His resignation comes amid a series of corruption scandals involving senior Ukrainian officials as Kyiv continues its war against Russia.

articles.title: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means
articles.summary: (First of two parts) MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has upheld a 2021 ruling that struck down a government regulation requiring commercial fishing vessels to be monitored electronically,…

blocks.text: (First of two parts)

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has upheld a 2021 ruling that struck down a government regulation requiring commercial fishing vessels to be monitored electronically, saying the measure went beyond what was reasonably necessary to fight illegal fishing and violated constitutional protections.

The ruling involved Fisheries Administrative Order (FAO) No. 266, issued by the Department of Agriculture (DA) through the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) in 2020. The order required Philippine-flagged commercial fishing vessels to install a Vessel Monitoring System (VMS) and use an Electronic Reporting System (ERS).
In an 82-page decision promulgated Jan. 21, 2026, the high court, voting 13-2, affirmed the June 1, 2021, decision of the Malabon City Regional Trial Court declaring FAO No. 266 unconstitutional.

blocks.caption: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

blocks.text: Graphics by Ed Lustan/Inquirer.net
The Supreme Court also directed the DA, through BFAR, to take “immediate steps to rectify deficiencies in Fisheries Administrative Order No. 266” and report the action taken to the court.
The decision was made public July 30.

But what exactly did the court find wrong with vessel monitoring? What does FAO No. 266 require? What does the Fisheries Code actually say about monitoring fishing vessels? And does the ruling mean commercial fishing vessels can now enter municipal waters without consequence?
Here’s what you need to know.
What is vessel monitoring?
Vessel Monitoring Measures (VMM) refer to systems used by fisheries authorities to monitor fishing vessels.
The Supreme Court decision describes the VMS as a system that “tracks, monitors, and manages fishing vessels,” while the ERS is used to record, report, process, store and transmit fisheries data.
Under FAO No. 266, commercial Philippine-flagged fishing vessels were required to use these systems.

The ERS was designed to electronically record information, including the species and volume of fish caught, the vessel’s position, and the date and time of fishing activity. The order also provided for the continuous transmission of vessel information while fishing.

blocks.caption: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

blocks.text: The regulation had several stated purposes, including improving the monitoring of fishing operations, strengthening law enforcement, supporting fisheries research and data collection, ensuring seafood traceability and catch documentation, assisting in the investigation of fisheries violations, and helping locate vessels during accidents and disasters.
In other words, VMM was not simply a GPS tracker. It was intended to give fisheries authorities electronic information about where vessels were, when they were fishing and what they were catching.
Why was FAO No. 266 issued?
The roots of the regulation go back to the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998, or Republic Act No. 8550.

The law was amended in 2015 by Republic Act No. 10654, which specifically sought to strengthen the prevention, deterrence and elimination of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, or IUUF. The amended law also strengthened the state’s mandate to manage Philippine fisheries sustainably.

The amended Fisheries Code says the state is to ensure the “rational and sustainable development, management and conservation” of fishery and aquatic resources while maintaining ecological balance and protecting the environment.
It also expressly requires a government monitoring, control and surveillance system.

blocks.caption: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

blocks.text: Section 14 of the amended Fisheries Code states:

“A monitoring, control and surveillance system shall be established by the Department in coordination with LGUs, FARMCs, the private sector and other agencies concerned to ensure that the fisheries and aquatic resources in Philippine waters are judiciously and wisely utilized and managed on a sustainable basis and conserved for the benefit and enjoyment exclusively of Filipino citizens.”
The same provision says:
“The [Monitoring, Control and Surveillance] system shall encompass all Philippine flagged fishing vessels regardless of fishing area and final destination of catch.”
There is another provision that is particularly relevant to the case.
Section 119 of the amended Fisheries Code says:

“No municipal, commercial or distant water fishing vessel shall engage in fishing activity without complying with the vessel monitoring measures promulgated by the Department in coordination with the LGUs.”
It also makes it unlawful to “intentionally tamper with, switch off or disable the vessel monitoring system.”

This wording is important because the Supreme Court did not strike down Sections 14 and 119 themselves. The case was about whether the DA and BFAR had validly implemented those provisions through FAO No. 266.
What changed under FAO No. 266?
Before FAO No. 266, the DA had issued FAO No. 260 in 2018.
FAO No. 260 applied VMM and ERS rules to commercial Philippine-flagged fishing vessels targeting “straddling and highly migratory fish stocks.”
FAO No. 266, issued Oct. 12, 2020, amended that order by removing that limitation.
“Thus, the rules and regulations henceforth were to apply to all commercial Philippine-flagged fishing vessels,” the Supreme Court ruling stated.
The expansion became the subject of a constitutional challenge by Royale Fishing Corporation, Bonanza Fishing and Market Resources Inc. and RBL Fishing Corporation.

blocks.caption: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

blocks.text: The companies argued that information gathered through VMS — including vessel locations and information about fishing grounds — could reveal commercially valuable information. They argued that compulsory monitoring also amounted to an unreasonable search and violated their rights to due process and equal protection.
They also argued that the regulation had been issued without the scientific study and stakeholder consultations required under the rules governing the implementation of the Fisheries Code.
The government disagreed.

Among other arguments, the Republic said abundant fishing grounds could already be located through modern technology and that the real-time location of fishing vessels could be tracked even without VMS using publicly available technologies, including satellite-based systems.

It also pointed out that fishing vessels were already required to report their “fish catch and spoilage, landing points, and quantity and value of fish caught, and off-loaded for transshipment, sale, and/or other disposal.”
What did the Supreme Court decide?
The Supreme Court did not say that fighting IUUF was an illegitimate government objective.
Instead, it examined whether the particular means used in FAO No. 266 were reasonably connected to that objective and whether the regulation stayed within the authority granted by law.
The court applied the rational basis test, which examines whether a government measure is reasonably related to a legitimate state interest.
The court also recognized the government’s interest in conserving marine resources and preventing illegal fishing. However, it found the 24/7 monitoring requirement unnecessarily restrictive.
One reason the court cited was that FAO No. 260 itself already provided another method for reporting a vessel’s position when the monitoring equipment was not working.
Section 22 of FAO No. 260 provided:
“In the event of a technical failure or non-functioning of the VMM on board the fishing vessel, the Master or Operator shall communicate this immediately to the FMC.”
It further required manual reporting every four hours through other communication channels, such as radio, phone or email, until the vessel returned to port.

blocks.caption: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

blocks.text: The Supreme Court found that these alternatives were less intrusive and concluded that the continuous monitoring requirement in FAO No. 266 was unduly restrictive.

“Indubitably, the availability of other means which are less intrusive and even more effective in preventing and detecting IUUF, makes the 24/7 monitoring required by FAO No. 266 unduly restrictive. VMS cannot even detect overfishing or unreported fishing,” the court stated.
The court consequently held that FAO No. 266 failed the rational basis test because the government had not shown that the chosen means were reasonable in relation to the interest being protected.
The decision also said:
“Equally established is that the expected output from VMS ‘is no different from the present manual reporting’ already being done by the fishing vessels.”

The court further said VMS could not effectively track unregistered or illegal fishers and that the Republic had failed to provide evidence showing that VMS was more effective — or even as effective as manual reporting — in preventing certain fishing violations.
What about fishing grounds being a trade secret?
This was another important part of the case.
The commercial fishing companies argued that information about where and when they fish can have commercial value.

The Supreme Court noted that they considered information such as the location of fishing vessels and the species thriving in a fishing ground at a certain point in time to be trade secrets, saying fishing companies spend heavily to identify fishing grounds and keep such information private.

The Supreme Court agreed that fishing activities could constitute trade secrets, ruling that “the fishing activities of the fisherfolk and the owners and operators of fishing vessels constitute trade secrets.” It clarified, however, that these are proprietary rights and not rights protected by the constitutional right to privacy.
The government, on the other hand, argued that modern technologies could already identify fishing grounds and track vessel locations.

It further argued that even if the information were considered trade secrets, it was “adequately protected” under Republic Act No. 8550, as amended, which categorizes the data as sensitive technical information and penalizes unauthorized disclosure.

blocks.caption: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

blocks.text: The court then examined whether FAO No. 266 could require the continuous collection and recording of such information. It found that the Fisheries Code does not require fishing operators to reveal all their fishing locations 24/7 and that the law’s definition of “monitoring” does not extend to the continuous tracking of vessel locations or destinations.

The distinction is important: The ruling recognized fishing-related information as proprietary, but the court’s decision turned on whether FAO No. 266 went beyond what the Fisheries Code authorized in requiring continuous monitoring and reporting.
For ocean conservation group Oceana, the privacy argument raised in the case overlooks the fact that commercial fishing takes place in waters owned and managed by the state.

“However, commercial fishers do not own the waters they work in. A fishing license is a privilege the State grants with conditions, and monitoring is one of them. Operators accept those terms when they receive the license,” Oceana said.
“They already hand over this same information through manual reporting, and information volunteered is no longer private,” it added.

Oceana argued that monitoring activity in a public resource should not be equated with searching the private affairs of an individual. In its view, commercial operators cannot treat portions of public waters as private spaces while exercising a state-granted privilege to fish there.
“You cannot claim privacy over waters you do not own,” Oceana stressed.
Why did the court consider the monitoring an unreasonable search?
The Supreme Court also examined the constitutional protection against unreasonable searches and seizures.
The court noted that one of FAO No. 266’s stated objectives was “to establish a system that will facilitate law enforcement and aid in case building and prosecution of fisheries law violations.”
Because VMS data could be used for law enforcement and prosecution, the court treated the compulsory collection of the information as raising search-and-seizure concerns.
The court said FAO No. 266 went beyond the parameters provided by the Fisheries Code.

It added that the amended law already requires commercial fishing vessels to maintain daily records of their catches and spoilage, landing points, and the quantity and value of fish caught and off-loaded for transshipment, sale or other disposal.
Section 38 provides:

“Each commercial fishing vessel shall keep a daily record of fish catch and spoilage, landing points, and quantity and value of fish caught, and off-loaded for transhipment, sale and/ or other disposal.”
It further requires the information to be certified by the vessel captain and transmitted to BFAR within the period prescribed by the implementing rules.

The Supreme Court found that the law did not expressly require commercial fishing operators to continuously disclose their fishing locations. For the court, FAO No. 266 therefore compelled the disclosure and recording of proprietary information beyond the statutory requirements.
“The monitoring, control, and surveillance system implemented by FAO No. 266 goes beyond what Republic Act No. 8550, as amended, authorizes,” the court stated.
Was there also a problem with consultations?

The government maintained that BFAR had conducted consultations with fishing vessel operators, local governments, the academe, experts, nongovernment organizations and fisherfolk before FAO No. 266 was issued.
It also presented evidence that the National Fisheries and Aquatic Resources Management Council had deliberated on the regulation.
But the Supreme Court examined the more specific requirements under the Fisheries Code’s implementing rules.

Those rules state that regulations must be based on scientific studies and that, in conducting such studies, affected stakeholders should be informed about the study, its duration and the experts conducting it. Stakeholders may also nominate scientists or comment on the experts involved.

The rules likewise require consultations in affected regions and at least 15 days’ prior notice of consultations, including publication of the notice in a newspaper of general circulation where feasible.

blocks.caption: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means

blocks.text: The Supreme Court found that the government had not shown compliance with all of those requirements.

The decision noted, among other things, that the scientific material relied upon by the government was a 2006 international expert consultation on VMS and that there had been no Philippines-specific scientific study conducted with stakeholder participation for FAO No. 266.

“Contrary to the argument of the Republic, the Republic’s discretion in choosing a scientific study upon which a regulation shall be based is subject to the following qualifications or limitations: first, the stakeholders in the affected region shall be informed of the conduct of the study, its duration and the expert/s who will conduct the same; second, the stakeholders must be given opportunity to nominate their own scientist/s to participate in the study, third, the stakeholders must be afforded the chance to provide comments on the scientist who will conduct the study,” the court said.

“None of these qualifications have been complied with by the Republic, considering that the sole scientific study relied upon by the Republic was released in 2006, or almost 15 years prior to the issuance of FAO No. 266,” it continued.
“Worse, the Republic did not even present the supposed scientific study to the stakeholders during the series of consultations that it conducted,” the court added.
The court therefore found a procedural due process problem in the regulation’s issuance.
Why did the court strike down FAO No. 266 instead of just changing it?

The Supreme Court found that the regulation failed the rational basis test and amounted to an unreasonable search and seizure. It also found violations involving the commercial fishing operators’ constitutional rights to due process and equal protection.
The court acknowledged that the government had legitimate reasons for issuing the order.
In the decision’s concluding discussion, it said:
“There is no doubt that the issuance of FAO No. 266 by the DA and the BFAR was driven by noble intentions.”
But the court continued:
“Nonetheless, the chosen manner of implementation has been shown to transgress fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution.”
It said the state’s interest could still be preserved through “lawful and less restrictive means.”
The Supreme Court consequently affirmed the Malabon RTC’s 2021 decision declaring FAO No. 266 null and void for being unconstitutional.

But the ruling does not end the government’s authority to regulate fishing — or erase the Fisheries Code’s vessel-monitoring requirements. The bigger question is what the decision means for the waters where commercial and municipal fishers operate, how authorities can enforce fishing restrictions without FAO No. 266, and why small-scale fishers and fisheries groups are now asking the Supreme Court to reconsider.

The second part of this explainer will examine what changes — and what does not — after the ruling, and why its implications extend from municipal waters and fisherfolk livelihoods to fisheries enforcement, seafood exports and the country’s continuing fisheries crisis. /dm

articles.title: PNP returns Romualdez arrest warrant to Sandiganbayan
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday returned the warrant of arrest for plunder of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez to the Sandiganbayan Third Division.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday returned the warrant of arrest for plunder of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez to the Sandiganbayan Third Division.
Romualdez did not appear before the court as he remained confined while under arrest at Cardinal Santos Memorial Medical Center in San Juan City.

“I brought the return of the warrant together with his medical evaluation conducted in Cardinal Santos,” PNP – Criminal Investigation and Detection Group chief Col. John Guiagui said in an ambush interview.
“We just had to return the warrant in the Third Division to inform them that the warrant has been served,” he added.
The police served Romualdez’s arrest warrant and the lawmaker also underwent booking procedures.
Romualdez on Monday filed an Urgent Motion ad Cautelam for Continued Hospital Confinement to the Third Division in a bid to extend his hospital confinement.
Romualdez said he was admitted to hospital on Monday due to Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism and other illnesses.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co and two others hours after the Office of the Ombudsman filed the information containing the formal charges against the accused.

According to the information containing the formal charges filed by prosecutors before the anti-graft court, Romualdez and Co were charged with “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen (15) occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.

The amount allegedly came from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025, according to the information.
Romualdez, in response, said he respects the legal process and will face the allegations against him in accordance with the law, according to his counsel Ade Fajardo. /gsg

articles.title: Retired teacher found dead in apparent drowning in Eastern Samar
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY— A 61-year-old retired teacher was found dead in the seawater off Barangay Mina-anod in Llorente, Eastern Samar, on Monday evening, in what police are investigating as an apparent…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY— A 61-year-old retired teacher was found dead in the seawater off Barangay Mina-anod in Llorente, Eastern Samar, on Monday evening, in what police are investigating as an apparent drowning.
The victim, identified by police as alias “Leo,” a resident of Barangay Mina-anod, was found floating face down in the sea at 6:10 p.m., according to the Llorente Municipal Police Station.
Police said a fisherman identified the man floating in the waters and alerted authorities.
Personnel from the Llorente police and Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office responded to the area and recovered the victim.
The victim was brought to Llorente Medical Hospital (Medicare), where an attending physician declared him dead.
Initial police investigation showed that at around 3 a.m. on the same day, a resident saw the victim arrive at Barangay So-ong aboard a small boat while transporting visitors.
The victim and his passengers reportedly docked at the barangay, after which the victim left alone aboard the same boat. That was the last time he was seen alive.
Police said the victim’s immediate family later identified the body as that of Leo.
An initial examination showed no apparent physical injuries or indications of foul play, police said.
Authorities are continuing their investigation to determine the circumstances./coa

articles.title: Lucena teen, older companion shot dead while hunting spiders
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — A fifteen-year-old boy was killed alongside a 26-year-old companion while their group of friends scavenged for spiders on Monday night. According to a spot report from the Lucena City…

blocks.text: LUCENA CITY — A fifteen-year-old boy was killed alongside a 26-year-old companion while their group of friends scavenged for spiders on Monday night.

According to a spot report from the Lucena City police, the victims were out hunting for spiders with four other friends in Purok Jasmine, Barangay Domoit when they were assaulted by a suspect at 10:30 p.m.
Police said a 38-year-old farm manager – without apparent reason or provocation – allegedly fired a shotgun, killing the boy and the older victim.
The four other companions scampered away after hearing the gunshots.

Investigators recovered two empty shotgun shells at the crime scene and later arrested the gunman. No further details about the attack or the motive for shooting the teenager and his companion were available at presstime./coa

articles.title: Gen Z uprising reshaped Nepal’s politics. A year on, questions linger
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Rakesh Mahato lies in a hospital bed in Kathmandu with a simple wish—to get up, take a few steps and make it home. The 25-year-old from Sarlahi district has spent the entirety of…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Rakesh Mahato lies in a hospital bed in Kathmandu with a simple wish—to get up, take a few steps and make it home.
The 25-year-old from Sarlahi district has spent the entirety of the past year in hospital after being shot by police while protesting against corruption on September 8, 2025.

Mahato is among the thousands injured during the youth-led uprising, which has come to be known as the Gen Z protests. Although the immediate trigger was the KP Sharma Oli government’s ban on social media, the youth were protesting systemic corruption and decades of power-sharing among a small group of ageing politicians.

The protests began as a peaceful demonstration but soon spiralled out of control, leading to massive casualties and the loss of private and public property. As many as 76 people were killed and 2,638 were injured during the demonstrations on September 8 and the violence that followed the next day. The spontaneous protests became a historic political event—triggering a major upheaval in the young democracy and turning the lives of thousands, including Mahato’s, upside down.
People, however, have yet to see the promises of the monumental movement translate into their daily lives, activists who took part in the protests say.

The faces in Singha Durbar, the country’s administrative centre, have changed. For the injured and families of those killed, however, life remains frozen on the two days of the uprising. Kantipur spoke to nearly a dozen people affected by the protests. Their demands were strikingly consistent—an end to corruption, better governance and a state that answers to its citizens. The movement transformed Nepal’s political leadership. Shah, once mayor of Kathmandu, became prime minister after the election. The party secured a near two-thirds majority. But for those who bled on the streets, little has changed, Mahato says.

blocks.caption: Prakash Bohora, 29, from Dailekh, became a symbol of the Gen Z uprising after an image of his blood-stained white shoes went viral. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Mahato was one of thousands of ambitious young men who travel to Kathmandu every year from across Nepal, seeking opportunities beyond their rural villages and small towns. He was studying for a bachelor’s degree at a commerce college and preparing for Loksewa, Nepal’s civil service examinations. He hoped to support his struggling family, get his younger brother a good education and make it big himself. Even in the capital city, jobs were scarce and the economy was in freefall. Like thousands of others, the Mahato brothers grew disillusioned by what they saw. Attributing these systemic issues to entrenched corruption, nepotism, and favouritism, they joined the protests together.

The demonstration was peaceful until shortly after noon, when gunfire suddenly erupted. One protester, Dipendra Basnet, was shot in the head in front of Parliament. Mahato and others rushed to help him. “That’s when police opened fire from behind,” Mahato recalled to Kantipur from his hospital bed. “I was shot in the belly and then I collapsed on the spot.”

The bullet entered through the right side of his abdomen and lodged on the left. Mahato regained consciousness three days later. By then, the protests had already set in motion a dramatic political transition. Gen Z representatives had proposed former chief justice Sushila Karki as interim prime minister during talks with army chief Ashok Raj Sigdel, while discussions were under way at the president’s office over forming a new government.

Mahato, meanwhile, was struggling to move his legs in the intensive care unit at the National Trauma Centre. He could not. A doctor eventually told him that he would never walk again and would probably depend on a wheelchair for the rest of his life. The nerves below his waist had been severed.
Mahato was devastated.

On September 12, four days after Oli resigned, an interim government was formed under Karki, following the violent uprising. Six months later, parliamentary elections brought the Rastriya Swatantra Party to a near two-thirds majority, and Balendra Shah, the rapper, structural engineer and former mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, became the prime minister. That a 35-year-old political novice had become the prime minister was a tectonic shift for the country’s politics dominated by a handful of geriatric men.
Mahato watched from his hospital bed as Shah took office. He was hopeful.

A year later, that hope has receded. “They haven’t even investigated who shot us and why,” Mahato said. “No one has been punished. Sometimes it feels like this government is no different from the previous ones.”

An inquiry led by former chief justice Gauri Bahadur Karki concluded that police had used excessive and indiscriminate force during the protests. The panel said security forces fired continuously for about four hours before a curfew was imposed and that the police and the political leadership failed to intervene.

The report prompted police to arrest former prime minister Oli and former home minister Ramesh Lekhak on charges linked to the deaths during the crackdown. Shah’s first Cabinet meeting had decided to implement the inquiry’s recommendations. The two were later released after the Supreme Court considered a habeas corpus petition.
But police have yet to file a case against them. Home Minister Sudan Gurung told Kantipur recently that investigators were gathering enough evidence.

For the injured protesters, however, the legal process offers little comfort. Many say the government has failed to honour earlier commitments to provide full medical treatment, jobs for one family member of the injured and employment suited to injured protesters’ qualifications.
For some, life has become unbearable.

An agreement reached between the Gen Z representatives and Karki’s interim government on December 10 said the state would establish a permanent body to promote integrity and good governance, fight corruption and end impunity. It also promised an emergency task force to address the immediate and long-term needs of families of those killed and injured, including compensation, free medical care and psychological counselling, education, employment, social security and a permanent memorial.
Many now say the government has forgotten those promises.

blocks.caption: Kamal Ghimire was discharged around mid-December last year. He now regrets taking part in the protest. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Kamal Ghimire of Kavre still carries the scars of a gunshot wound to his chest. He has become accustomed to the physical pain. But the disappointment is harder to bear, he says. “Doctors had said I might not survive, and that’s perhaps why the wound no longer hurts as much,” he said. “But my heart hurts. I feel that this pain will stay with me for the rest of my life…They call this a Gen Z government. Then why have they forgotten the injured?”

Ghimire was discharged around mid-December last year. He now regrets taking part in the protest. “Those who went into government came out untouched,” he said. “Their lives carried on as normal. We’re the ones left with ruined bodies and no way to rebuild our lives. We can’t go abroad to seek work, and there’s little we can do here. So what do we gain from the movement if the government still can’t give us proper access to education, healthcare or jobs?”

The government had promised to cover Ghimire’s medical expenses. Yet he says he has been paying for follow-up treatment himself and previously had to buy medicines outside the hospital. His family has spent about Rs1.5 million on his treatment, he said.

Shree Krishna Shrestha, an additional secretary at the Ministry of Health, said the government could not reimburse bills for medicines or treatment bought independently outside the designated hospital system. Under government rules, hospitals treating injured protesters must submit claims themselves, he said.

According to Health Ministry figures, one Gen Z protester, Daulat Thapa, is still being treated at the Kathmandu Medical College in Sinamangal. “He is still in a coma and is receiving intensive care, but there has been no improvement,” Shrestha said. Mahato continues to receive regular physiotherapy.
For others, the financial burden is becoming overwhelming.

blocks.caption: Bhandari lives in a rented room in Lokanthali and counts the days until his next hospital visit. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Rabi Bhandari, 29, from Sindhuli, survived a gunshot to the leg. But survival has not felt like a victory. At times, he says, he wonders whether it would have been easier to be among the 76 protesters who were killed.

Bhandari lives in a rented room in Lokanthali and counts the days until his next hospital visit. But every appointment brings the same question: how will he pay the bills? He was treated at B&B Hospital, where staff have told him he will now have to pay for treatment.

Additional Secretary Shrestha said the government prefers public hospitals because private treatment can be prohibitively expensive. But he acknowledged that officials were considering how to address cases involving protesters treated in private facilities.

Karki’s interim government had also introduced a system to classify injured protesters according to the severity of their disabilities. Those classified as very seriously injured receive a monthly allowance of Rs18,000, those in the serious category Rs9,000, and those classified as moderately or mildly injured Rs4,000.

Bhandari says the classification was poorly handled. “Many people were placed in the moderate or mild categories without properly examining their injuries and medical reports,” he said. “I was initially classified as moderate. I kept appealing, and only this year was I moved to the serious category.”

He now receives Rs9,000 a month. “But what can you do with Rs9,000?” he said. He has received only the monthly subsistence allowance and an additional Rs35,000 from the government so far. “The allowance does not even cover my rent,” he said.

Law Minister Sobita Gautam said the government was doing what it could within its authority. She said the government was also helping protesters who had travelled to India for treatment and was committed to providing free treatment within Nepal.
The frustrations extend beyond healthcare.

Ambika BK, from Udayapur, took a contract job in the administration section of the Nepal Electricity Authority’s Ratnapark office two months ago. But with limited pay and few benefits, the job has done little to ease the financial strain. “Most of what I earn, around Rs20,000 to Rs22,000, goes on rent and food,” she said. “There’s hardly anything left for my children’s education and healthcare.”

The job has brought another source of pain. She says people sometimes insult her in front of her colleagues, saying she got the job only because her husband died in the protest. “Sometimes I feel like quitting because of that,” she said.

BK’s husband, Santosh, was 28 and worked in a jewellery factory. On the morning of September 8, he returned home for lunch after work. He told his wife that the Oli government had shut down social media and that a peaceful protest was taking place.
“We have to go,” he told her. He left home at around 11.30am.
He never returned.

BK says the government that came to power on the back of the Gen Z movement has given families like hers little reason for hope. “Most of what was done happened under Sushila Karki’s government,” she said. “The government that followed has barely cared about the families of those killed.” She added she sent 14 or 15 demands through Home Minister Sudan Gurung but received no meaningful response.

She also holds Shah responsible. “Balen did not even visit the injured in hospital or pay tribute to the dead,” she said. “Promises about free education, healthcare and jobs for our children remain unfulfilled.”
Her children were eventually offered free education through grade 12 by Golden Peak Group.
For BK, that has not erased the loss. She often breaks down while looking at her husband’s photograph hanging on the wall.

The organisations representing the injured and bereaved families say the government’s record is equally disappointing. Gen Z leader Sarisma Thapa said several demands, including the creation of a Gen Z council, remain unresolved. “Even getting identity cards issued to injured protesters took sustained pressure,” she said. “Some people have been kept in limbo with token offers of jobs in government offices, on contracts or as administrative assistants.”

Despite the promise of free treatment, she said many injured protesters still have to buy medicines themselves beyond what public hospitals provide. She also said young protesters arrested in connection with the unrest remain in jail even though the government had agreed not to prosecute people simply for participating in the demonstrations.
For the families of those killed and the protesters who survived, September 8 remains an event that continues to shape daily life.

blocks.caption: Ambika BK, from Udayapur, took a contract job in the administration section of the Nepal Electricity Authority’s Ratnapark office two months ago. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Roshan Gautam, secretary of the Gen Z Martyrs’ Families Welfare Society, said the government had effectively abandoned them. “The prime minister has not even met the families of the dead and injured once,” he said. “Compensation is still a distant prospect.”

Some injured protesters also tried to turn their place in the movement into a role in Parliament, government or the ruling party. Prakash Bohora, 29, from Dailekh, was one of them. He became a symbol of the Gen Z uprising after an image of his blood-stained white shoes went viral. But he never secured a political role.

Bohora now relies on crutches to walk, and even passing through New Baneshwar can bring back painful memories. “Sometimes, when I pass the parliament building, it still hurts,” he said. “I find myself wishing I never had to go there.”

He is now staying at a hostel in Kathmandu while making regular follow-up visits to Bir Hospital. He still needs four more operations on his left leg, which was shot during the protests on September 8. He was discharged only five months later, on February 3.

Bohora contested the parliamentary election on a proportional-representation ticket for the Rastriya Swatantra Party but was not elected. He later ran for the party’s central committee at its general convention in Chitwan, but lost.

He is now frustrated by the absence of Gen Z victims in both government and Parliament. Their lack of representation, he says, has left their grievances easier to ignore. “But we will not stop asking questions until the demands and issues we raised are addressed,” he said. “And if the government forgets what citizens expected from this movement, we will continue to hold it to account.”
Even those who joined the protests and survived are wondering whether the movement will actually change their future.

Dhiraj Joshi, a Gen Z protester who took part in talks at the Nepali Army headquarters in the early hours of September 9, said protesters never took to the streets expecting to be injured, killed or rewarded. “No one joins a protest thinking they will be injured, killed or honoured,” he said. “But once people have been killed and injured, the government has a responsibility to honour the commitments it made.”

The movement was ultimately driven by demands for accountability, transparency and an end to corruption, Joshi said. Those in power must also recognise the sacrifices made by the injured and the families of those killed, he added. “A year on, it does not feel like the government is moving towards greater accountability,” Joshi told Kantipur. “The government appears to be falling short on accountability, responsibility and democratic values.”

Law Minister Sobita Gautam said the government was in regular contact with injured protesters and families of those killed and that the Gen Z Council would provide a more formal channel for that engagement.

“It’s not that we have stopped talking to them,” she said. “But it can sometimes be difficult to speak to everyone individually. That is why we want the Gen Z Council to serve as a channel through which their concerns can reach the government.”

She said the government was already in direct talks with the affected families and protesters and acknowledged their frustration over the delays. “Understandably, they feel things are taking too long,” she said. “But we needed time to work out how to implement the agreements and set up the necessary mechanisms. That work is under way, and it should not take much longer.”
Meanwhile, a year after rallying in Kathmandu for a corruption-free Nepal, injured protesters say they are left with little more than frustration and regret.

Mahato, who was shot in the belly and collapsed on the spot, says he is disappointed that the current government hasn’t investigated who shot them and why. He adds he keeps repeating the same question to himself: “When will I be able to stand and walk again?”
Bhandari, who sustained a gunshot in his leg, says he regrets his decision to join the protests. “Sometimes I ask myself why the bullet hit my leg,” he says. “Why didn’t it hit my chest?” /dl

articles.title: Russia, North Korea open first road bridge across border
articles.summary: SEOUL — North Korea called the first road bridge across its narrow border with Russia a concrete sign of tightening bonds, state media reported Tuesday, as the Ukraine war draws the…

blocks.text: SEOUL — North Korea called the first road bridge across its narrow border with Russia a concrete sign of tightening bonds, state media reported Tuesday, as the Ukraine war draws the Western-sanctioned nations closer.
The bridge over the Tumen river, which Russia said is designed to accommodate a projected growth in freight and passenger traffic, adds to the rail and air links between the neighbours.
The ceremony on Monday marking its opening came as Russia and North Korea have heavily boosted military and economic ties since Moscow launched its Ukraine offensive in 2022.

“The completion of the bridge is a significant event adding a new dynamic movement to the overall bilateral cooperation,” North Korean official Pak Thae Song said, according the official KCNA news agency.
Video published by the Russian government showed trucks from both sides crossing the bridge, as crowds lining the road applauded.
“The launch of the first automobile route will further strengthen the connection between our friendly countries,” Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in a video link at the ceremony.

KCNA added that the new bridge ensures “safe passage of various forms of transport and the movement of people,” and has “strengthened a key infrastructure component for economic cooperation between North Korea and Russia.”

North Korea dispatched thousands of troops to Russia in 2024 to help ward off a Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region, while Kyiv has accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles in its nightly barrages.
The two countries signed a defence treaty in 2024 that provides for mutual support if either country is attacked.
One of the world’s most isolated and repressive countries, North Korea bars most its citizens from leaving and heavily monitors incoming travellers.
Russian tourism to North Korea has increased in recent years, although Pyongyang sometimes closes its border at short notice.

South Korea’s central bank estimated in July that North Korea’s economy grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, citing it’s expansion of economic cooperation with Russia as a “major drive.”
The bank’s official said North Korea’s gross national income also “received a boost from a sharp rise in foreign currency earnings” linked to the deployment of its troops to Russia.

Ukrainian rights group Truth Hounds, meanwhile, previously warned that the new bridge could become “a direct artery for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, with Russian technology and resources flowing in the opposite direction”. /dl

articles.title: Sison opposes Sara Duterte testifying in her own impeachment trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s lead defense counsel Atty. Sheila Sison invoked a Constitutional provision prohibiting the accused from testifying against his or her own trial,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s lead defense counsel Atty. Sheila Sison invoked a Constitutional provision prohibiting the accused from testifying against his or her own trial, after the prosecution team said they intend to call Duterte as a witness.
“There is an innate problem in that kind of request… because the Constitution prohibits this kind of testimonial compulsion from the accused herself,” Sison said.

Sison made the statement on day 23 of the impeachment trial of Duterte in response to a manifestation made by prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan where she announced that they intend to call Duterte to the witness stand, at the appropriate time.

This, after the Kapunan likewise announced that the prosecution team are foregoing the 15 remaining witnesses for Article I, or the alleged misuse, misappropriation, and irregular liquidation of confidential funds.
According to Sison, Article III, Section 17 of the 1987 Constitution puts in a “guarantee” that “no person should be compelled to testify against himself or herself.”
“This is a fundamental right” from the Constitution itself, that protects not just the vice president but any Filipino, she added.
Sison, however, said the defense team reserves their right to formally comment on the matter once the prosecution team makes a formal motion or request to subpoena Duterte.

Despite the prosecution’s repeated calls for Duterte to appear before the impeachment court, Sison likewise reiterated their stance since the trials began in July that Duterte is amply represented by her lawyers.

“It is clear that the respondent is here, through her counsel. If the Respondent is not interested in this trial, she would not have even sent her lawyers to defend her in this case,” Sison said. /jpv

articles.title: Sara Duterte can't be compelled to testify at impeachment trial --defense lawyer
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte cannot be compelled to testify against herself during her own impeachment trial, her lead defense counsel said Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 11:09am
Vice President Sara Duterte cannot be compelled to testify against herself during her own impeachment trial, her lead defense counsel said Tuesday.
During the 23rd day of the impeachment trial, lawyer Sheila Sison cited Section 17, Article 3 of the Constitution, which states that “no person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.”

“This right is absolute and this is not only a simple right or a statutory right. This is a fundamental right. This is a right emanating from the Constitution itself and one that emanates from the guarantees under Article 3 of our 1987 Constitution,” she said.
This came after the House Prosecution panel said they intend to call Duterte to the witness stand.
Sison also said that Duterte is present in the trial through her counsel.
“If respondent is not interested in this trial, she would not have even sent her lawyers to defend her in this case,” she said.
Meanwhile, the prosecution also said it would forego the presentation of witnesses for Article 1 of the impeachment case, referring to the alleged misuse of confidential funds.

Duterte was impeached by the House of Representatives on May 11, in a vote of 257-25-9, on allegations of culpable violation of the 1987 Constitution, graft and corruption, betrayal of public trust, bribery, and other high crimes.
Her impeachment trial at the Senate impeachment court began on July 8. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Romualdez transfer to PNP General Hospital sought
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) will ask the court to allow the transfer of former speaker Martin Romualdez from a private hospital in San Juan City to PNP General Hospital at Camp Crame in…

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 11:08am

The Philippine National Police (PNP) will ask the court to allow the transfer of former speaker Martin Romualdez from a private hospital in San Juan City to PNP General Hospital at Camp Crame in Quezon City.
"Meantime, kami po ay magmo-motion for custody ni Martin Romualdez para dalhin sa Camp Crame hospital," Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said at a press briefing on Tuesday.
(For the meantime, we will be filing a motion for custody of Martin Romualdez to be taken to Camp Crame hospital.)
According to Remulla, the motion is expected to be filed either later Tuesday or Wednesday.
Romualdez was confined at a private hospital in San Juan City when authorities served his arrest warrant there on Monday evening.
Since Romualdez is considered a flight risk, Remulla said armed guards have been deployed at the San Juan City hospital.
"Dalawa ang kanyang private jet, tatlong ang kanyang helicopter, tatlo ang kanyang yacht. He is a flight risk," Remulla said.
(He has two private jets, three helicopters, and three yachts. He is a flight risk.)
According to Remulla, the PNP and the private hospital doctors agreed that Romualdez's condition is unstable. The former House Speaker reportedly suffered a stroke in July.
While Romualdez remains at the private hospital, PNP doctors will visit him daily to monitor his condition.

Remulla said Romualdez would eventually be brought before the Sandiganbayan once he is medically fit for trial. Authorities are also planning to seek his commitment to the Quezon City Jail in Payatas. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Who is lawyer Lorna Patajo-Kapunan?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Veteran lawyer Lorna Patajo-Kapunan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Kapunan has drawn…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Veteran lawyer Lorna Patajo-Kapunan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Kapunan has drawn attention during the proceedings for her courtroom style and quick-witted remarks. She has led the prosecution’s examination of witnesses, at times prompting laughter from the otherwise serious impeachment court.

With 48 years of legal practice, Kapunan specializes in litigation, intellectual property, licensing, franchising, corporate and commercial law, mergers and acquisitions, international humanitarian law, criminal law, family law and estate law.
Kapunan also teaches family law, media and the client, and the Code of Responsibility for Mandatory Continuing Legal Education (MCLE).
Kapunan is an advocate for women’s and children’s rights, environmental protection and LGBTQ rights.

She has served as a senior associate at ACCRA Law Office and as senior partner at Rico Robles Kapunan Law. She also founded Kapunan & Castillo Law Offices, where she has been a senior partner since 2011.
Kapunan earned her Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and Bachelor of Laws degrees from the University of the Philippines.

She also completed courses and seminars in international humanitarian law, intellectual property and invention and innovation, including programs at Magdalene College, Cambridge University, the International Institute of Humanitarian Law in San Remo, Italy, and the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Asian Region Seminar in Tajon, Republic of Korea.
Kapunan likewise served as a Bar examiner for Commercial Law in 1988./dp

articles.title: Nepal flood death toll rises to 1,355, nearly 5,000 unaccounted for
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The confirmed death toll from catastrophic flash floods in northern Nepal has risen to 1,355, with 4,996 people still unaccounted for, according to government data released on…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The confirmed death toll from catastrophic flash floods in northern Nepal has risen to 1,355, with 4,996 people still unaccounted for, according to government data released on Monday.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said search and rescue teams had recovered 1,355 bodies from eight districts following the late-August floods. Chitwan recorded the highest number of fatalities with 363, followed by Nawalparasi East with 222 and Nawalparasi West with 221.
Of those still unaccounted for, 2,340 are from Nuwakot and 1,967 from Rasuwa. The figure also includes 589 foreign nationals and around 100 security and government personnel.

Emergency teams have rescued 13,396 people so far. More than 21,000 security personnel remain deployed in the worst-hit mountain areas, including 9,287 soldiers from the Nepali Army, 7,912 personnel from the Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force. Preliminary estimates put losses to property, housing and infrastructure at Rs387.5 billion ($2.56 billion).

Helicopters have been crucial in reaching isolated areas of the Himalayas. Military, paramilitary and private operators based in Kathmandu have carried out nearly 1,500 flights to deliver supplies and evacuate survivors.

The government has allocated Rs160 million ($1.06 million) in emergency funds to affected district offices and municipal councils. More than 3,500 displaced people are being housed in 39 holding centers, while medical teams have treated 6,672 injured people.

Restoration of essential infrastructure is under way. Electricity has been restored to more than 78 percent of households in Rasuwa, over 96 percent in Nuwakot and more than 99 percent in Dhading. Telecommunications operators have also restored nearly 98 percent of damaged mobile towers.
Humanitarian agencies say difficult access and damaged roads remain the main obstacles to delivering heavy equipment and sustaining relief operations in remote parts of the affected districts. /dl

articles.title: Kapunan: Prosecution panel to call VP Sara Duterte to witness stand
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — In lieu of the other witnesses for Article I of the Articles of Impeachment, the prosecution panel will call Vice President Sara Duterte before the witness stand to clarify…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — In lieu of the other witnesses for Article I of the Articles of Impeachment, the prosecution panel will call Vice President Sara Duterte before the witness stand to clarify matters regarding different issues, including alleged confidential fund misuse.

In her manifestation on Tuesday, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said that they are forgoing the presentation of 15 of 27 witnesses for Article I, and instead reserves the right to summon Duterte before the Senate Impeachment Court to quiz her about all articles.

“Originally your Honor prosecution intended and this is so stated in our pretrial brief, 27 witnesses […] thus far we presented 10, and stipulated two other witnesses, rendering unnecessary their personal presence in court. All these lead — that’s why I started with a metaphor of all of these actors in the chess board, point to only one person,” Kapunan said during the trial on Tuesday.

“All of these pawns and castles and horses and bishop, point to only one person, and that accountable person is the Vice President. And that is why your Honor, in lieu of presenting 15 other witnesses, we will be presenting the Vice President herself as regards misuse, misappropriation of confidential funds, which is Article I of the Articles of Impeachment,” she added.

When asked by Presiding Officer and Senator-judge Francis Escudero if they will ask for a subpoena for Duterte, Kapunan explained that they will not yet seek one since they will be calling the Vice President at the end of the presentation of all articles.

“And as well we have two remaining Articles your Honor, the article on unexplained wealth and bribery, all of which unless the Vice President herself appears and respects the process of this impeachment court and affirms, confirms her allegation of innocence your Honor,” Kapunan said.

“Not at this time your Honor […] the testimony of the Vice President will be material to all four articles, the article on grave threats, Article IV, Article I on misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds, Article II on unexplained wealth, and Article III on bribery. And that is why, at the end of all of these articles, we reserve the right to present the Vice President herself,” she added.

The prosecution has finished presenting evidence and witnesses for Article IV or the allegation that Duterte betrayed public trust when she threatened President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his relatives.

As of Tuesday, 12 witnesses have been presented for Article I. Last week, lead public prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said they are looking to wrap up discussions for Article I by Wednesday, September 9. /jpv

articles.title: LOOK: DILG releases mugshot of hospitalized Romualdez
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Tuesday released the official mugshot of former House Speaker and Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Tuesday released the official mugshot of former House Speaker and Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez following his arrest over a plunder case.

The photo, presented during a press briefing in Camp Crame, shows Romualdez lying in a hospital bed at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, wearing a medical gown, nasal and an intravenous cannula.
Instead of wearing the standard orange Philippine National Police–Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP-CIDG) detainee shirt, Romualdez is seen with the shirt placed over his medical gown.
Romualdez was arrested on Monday night following a Sandiganbayan Third Division order.
He was charged with plunder in connection with over P7 billion worth of alleged kickbacks in various government projects from 2022 to 2025.

The PNP–CIDG National Capital Region previously explained that Romualdez could not be made to stand up for the mugshot nor wear the orange detainee shirt due to the medical apparatus attached to his body./dp

articles.title: A flood of bad news leaves Nepal’s tourist hubs eerily quiet
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The impact of the floods in the Bhotekoshi River is beginning to ripple through Nepal’s tourist industry, with hotels reporting a wave of cancellations just as the peak autumn…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The impact of the floods in the Bhotekoshi River is beginning to ripple through Nepal’s tourist industry, with hotels reporting a wave of cancellations just as the peak autumn tourist season gets underway.

Hotels in Pokhara, Chitwan and Lumbini say domestic and foreign tourists have cancelled their bookings following reports that have portrayed Nepal as unsafe in the wake of the August 26 disaster. Domestic travellers have also called off their plans because of difficult road conditions.
As a result, hotels in some of the country’s major tourist destinations are largely deserted during what is normally one of the busiest times of the year.

Sauraha in Chitwan, for instance, would be bustling with tourists at this time of year. This year, however, only a handful of tourists can be seen in the popular jungle destination. The Regional Hotel Association said hotel occupancy has fallen below 5 percent.
“There are hardly any tourists at the moment,” said Suman Ghimire, former president of the Regional Hotel Association Sauraha. “Hotel occupancy is below 5 percent.”

Ghimire’s Jungle Safari Lodge has 34 rooms. But after bookings were cancelled, most of the rooms are now empty, he said. Tourists have stopped travelling to Chitwan by road after the Krishnabhir section of the highway was washed away by floods.
Although the Bhotekoshi flood did not cause any damage in Chitwan, Ghimire said the destination was suffering because negative reports about Nepal had spread through travel advisories.
“There is no problem on the East-West Highway,” he said. “But tourism has been hit because reports have spread internationally portraying the situation in Nepal as disastrous.”

As alternatives to the damaged Mugling-Kathmandu section of the Prithvi Highway, the Hetauda-Kathmandu road, also known as the Kanti Lokpath, the Tribhuvan Highway and the Hetauda-Kulekhani road are operational. Tourists can use these routes to reach Chitwan. There is also no difficulty in reaching Chitwan by air from Kathmandu to Bharatpur.
Royal Tulip Chitwan Hotel, operated by KTM Hospitality, has 65 rooms. Rameshwar Sah, chairman of Royal Tulip, said 80 percent of bookings have been cancelled so far.

“The tourism sector has been severely hit by the floods,” Sah said. “Although the destinations themselves have not been affected by the floods, rumors and misleading reports about the situation have had a significant impact.”
Sauraha has 125 small and large hotels with a combined capacity to accommodate 8,000 tourists a day.
Gunaraj Thapaliya, vice-president of the Regional Hotel Association, said the impact was particularly visible in Sauraha.
“Except for a handful of Chinese tourists, there are no visitors in Sauraha at the moment,” he said.

Large hotels in Patihani and Meghauli are also waiting for tourists to return. At the Soaltee Westend Chitwan Resort in Patihani, Bharatpur, the number of guests has dropped sharply since the floods, said Choplal Pandey, general manager of the hotel.

“We are receiving messages from foreign tourists cancelling their bookings one after another,” he said. “Forty percent of bookings have already been cancelled. We became more concerned when guests also began cancelling bookings made through November.”
Pokhara, the tourist city in Kaski district, has also not escaped the impact.
Hari Bhujel, chairman of the Tourism Council, said the Bhotekoshi floods and damage to the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir have added to the challenges facing tourism in Pokhara.
“The tourist season for foreign visitors has begun,” he said. “But up to 30 percent of hotel bookings have been cancelled at present.”

He said the closure of the Prithvi Highway, increased airfares, inadequate flights between Pokhara and Kathmandu and the continued charging of dollar-denominated fares to foreign tourists have directly affected tourism in Pokhara.
The damage at Krishnabhir has also affected the arrival of Indian tourists travelling from Sunauli to Pokhara, then to Muktinath and on to Pashupatinath, he said.

“With the recent increase in fuel prices making airfares more expensive, the arrival of domestic tourists is also expected to decline,” he said. “However, it is necessary to convey the message to foreign tourists that destinations other than the areas affected by the floods are safe.”
Lumbini, the birthplace of Buddha, has also begun to see fewer tourists.

Lilamani Sharma, president of the Lumbini Hotel Association, said foreign tourists travelling to Lumbini via Kathmandu have been cancelling their hotel bookings. Bookings made for the main October-November season are also being cancelled, he said.
He said bookings were being cancelled because information was being circulated abroad in a way that made it appear that Nepal as a whole had been affected by the floods.
“The problem travelling to and from Kathmandu is because one or two sections of the Mugling-Kathmandu road have been damaged,” he said. “Even that situation is gradually improving.”

Khim Shrestha, operator of Hotel Suramma in Lumbini, said the government should take the initiative to communicate through foreign diplomatic missions in Nepal and international media that the situation in the country is improving and that Nepal is eager to welcome foreign visitors.

Bhavishwar Adhikari, operational manager of Hotel Hokke, a four-star boutique hotel in Lumbini, said 100 room-nights booked on various dates over a two-month period have been cancelled. He said the tourism sector would be badly affected if the government failed to immediately communicate internationally that the situation in the country was normal.
Prakash Bhattarai, operator of Shakya Guest House, said the problem was being compounded by the failure to communicate accurate information.

“One or two problems seen on the roads should not be exaggerated,” he said. “The local and federal governments should prioritise both information dissemination and repair and maintenance work to revive the tourism sector.”

Chandra Prakash Shrestha, president of Hotel Association Nepal’s Lumbini Province chapter, said Indian tourists arriving on package tours through border points such as Belahiya to visit various destinations have also been affected.

Indian tourists come to visit religious sites in the high Himalayan region. Following reports that the Himalayan region had been devastated by floods, they are understood to have cancelled their bookings.
Although tourists continue to visit border towns and nearby destinations for short stays, Shrestha said there had been a sharp decline in tourists travelling on package tours.
The tourist bus park at Mustang Chowk in Pokhara, which normally sees a steady flow of passengers from morning until night, is now deserted.
Twenty-four buses used to leave the bus park for Kathmandu in the morning and eight at night.

According to Buddhi Sagar Paudel, an employee at the Mustang Chowk branch of Prithvi Highway Bus Operators Company, 14 tourist buses used to leave from Prithvi Chowk, eight from Lamachaur, two from Hemja and two from Zero Kilometre.
At present, only tourist buses travelling to Chitwan and Lumbini are operating.
The Nepal Association of Tour and Travel Agents (NATTA) Gandaki also inspected an alternative route to bypass Krishnabhir on Saturday.

Sangita Paudel, president of NATTA Gandaki, said the association studied a route that involves crossing a suspension bridge from Krishnabhir to reach Jyāmire on the opposite side and then travelling 11 kilometres to reach Benighat.

“A diversion is currently being constructed at Krishnabhir and it is expected to come into operation within a week,” Paudel said. “But it is uncertain how long it will remain operational. If it cannot operate for a long period, the Jyamire-Benighat route could serve as an alternative.”

She said an alternative was being sought because large vehicles cannot travel along the Tribhuvan Highway from Hetauda to Naubise. The disruption to tourist vehicles has directly affected nearly 1,000 business operators and workers, Paudel said.
Meanwhile, the Lumbini Development Trust has said Lumbini, the birthplace of peace, remains completely safe and open despite the difficult situation in the country caused by the Bhotekoshi floods.

In a statement issued on Sunday, the trust said Lumbini had not been affected by the floods or the disaster and that, at a time when people were engaged in relief, rescue and assistance efforts, the Buddhist values of compassion, loving-kindness and harmony remained equally relevant. Visiting Lumbini, it said, could be meaningful for those seeking a sense of peace and spiritual energy.

“The recent floods have not affected the greater Lumbini area,” said Himal Upreti, acting member-secretary of the Lumbini Development Trust. “Lumbini, Kapilvastu, Devdaha, Ramgram and other major tourist destinations remain open to visitors.”

“The Bhotekoshi flood has created a negative message that the entire country is experiencing fear and hardship,” he said. “That is why we have to reassure the international community that Lumbini is safe and accessible.” /dl

MANILA, Philippines — A proposed measure in the Senate seeks to grant hazard pay and additional benefits to media workers who face occupational hazards while performing their duties.

Senate Bill No. 2440, or the proposed Media Workers Hazard Pay Act, seeks to require employers of public and private media entities to provide a minimum P650 daily hazard pay for media workers assigned to dangerous, embattled, or disease-infested areas.

“Media workers working for government or private entities who are already enjoying similar benefits equal or superior to the above amount shall no longer be entitled to such hazard pay,” the bill read.
It also proposed to provide mandatory additional insurance to media personnel in the event of death or injury in the course of their duties.

Among the proposed additional insurance benefits are a death benefit worth up to P200,000 for each media worker, a disability benefit also worth up to P200,000, and medical insurance worth up to P100,000.

The proposed bill also included a clause for overtime work and night shift differential pay for media personnel who are required to work beyond the normal eight-hour duty and for those who work between 10:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. the next day.

The bill said the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) will coordinate with the Civil Service Commission and other relevant agencies to establish the guidelines to accredit media workers for such benefits.
The bill was filed by Sen. Mark Villar, who cited the role of the media in providing information to the public during challenging conditions, such as in the middle of conflicts and rough weather.

“Media workers serve as the eyes and ears of the public during the most difficult and dangerous situations. If we expect them to face danger to keep our fellow citizens safe and well-informed, it is also our duty to ensure that they are protected, insured, and fairly compensated,” Villar said in a statement.

articles.title: Prosecution intends to present Sara Duterte in her own impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Tuesday said they intend to present Vice President Sara Duterte herself in her own impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 10:57am
The House prosecution panel on Tuesday said they intend to present Vice President Sara Duterte herself in her own impeachment trial.

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan informed the Senate impeachment court of such position during Day 23 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President as the prosecution rested the presentation of evidence on Article 1 of the Articles of Impeachment which alleges that the Vice President must be impeached over misuse, if not misappropriation of P612.5 million worth of confidential funds.
Kapunan, however, said that they are not asking Senate impeachment court for a subpoena for the Vice President "at this time."

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, in response, said issuing a subpoena or “testimonial compulsion” to the Vice President before her impeachment trial violates her Constitutional right as provided under Article 3, Section 17 which states that “No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.”

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Senator Francis Escudero did not yet rule on the move by the prosecution pending the latter’s formal motion asking the impeachment court to issue a subpoena to the Vice President and the comment from the defense panel. —VAL, GMA News

articles.summary: The individuals who were named as co-accused of former speaker and incumbent Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez in a plunder case could not be found at their original addresses, the…

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 10:47am

The individuals who were named as co-accused of former speaker and incumbent Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez in a plunder case could not be found at their original addresses, the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP-CIDG) said Tuesday.
This was revealed by PNP-CIDG National Capital Region chief Colonel John Guiagui, according to GMA News reporter Maki Pulido.

Romualdez's co-accused in the plunder charge filed Monday by the Office of the Ombudsman with the Sandiganbayan are former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co of Ako Bicol party-list; Romualdez's personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño; and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation.
Co, who is also facing other charges in connection with the flood control mess, was last reported to be staying in Paris, France, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said last May.
The Office of the Ombudsman on Monday morning filed the P7.4-billion plunder charge against Romualdez and three others over their alleged involvement in a kickback scheme on flood control projects.

“By repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least 15 occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, 'commitments' and/or other pecuniary benefits aggregating at least P7.4 billion by reason or on account of the respective public offices and positions of Romualdez and Co, including monies derived from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025, which monies were delivered to properties owned by, occupied by, or associated with Romualdez and received by Sereño and other persons acting for and in his behalf,” the criminal information read.
Likewise, Ombudsman prosecutors alleged that the P7.4 billion allowed Romualdez to acquire several assets.
Romualdez meanwhile was arrested Monday and has undergone the booking procedure at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center, Interior Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla said on Monday night.
The PNP-CIDG on Tuesday returned the arrest warrant issued for Romualdez to the Sandiganbayan.
Romualdez is now under their custody, the PNP-CIDG said. —with a report from Joahna Lei Casilao/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Prosecution drops remaining witnesses for alleged misuse of confi funds
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Tuesday said that it would forego the presentation of witnesses for Article 1 of the impeachment case, referring to the alleged misuse of confidential funds.

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 8, 2026 10:31am Updated September 8, 2026 11:40am

The House prosecution panel on Tuesday said that it would forego the presentation of the remaining 15 witnesses for Article 1 of the impeachment case, referring to the alleged misuse of confidential funds by Vice President Sara Duterte.
Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan announced this on the 23rd day of the trial.
“To date, we have already presented 10 witnesses and stipulated as to the testimony of 2 witnesses. So a total of 12 witnesses out of 27 witnesses," Kapunan said.

“After a long meeting last night and towards this morning, just before this hearing, the prosecution both public and private prosecutors, have decided today…we have decided to forego, Your Honors, not only with the witnesses subpoenaed for today, but with all the remaining 15 witnesses,” she added.
For Article 1, Kapunan said the prosecution initially intended to present a total of 27 witnesses and thousands of exhibits.
She explained that the decision was made due to the prosecution’s contention that the case “has become very clear.”

“Not a conclusion of fact and law, but a conclusion based on 4,750 documents presented and identified by the 12 witnesses---10 of whom were present in court and subjected themselves to long cross-examinations by the defense counsels, and as well to questions from the senator-jduges,” Kapunan said.
“The testimony elicited very clearly a pattern as one would see a chessboard,” she added, emphasizing the importance of Queen as a piece in the game.
Kapunan thus said the prosecution seeks to present Duterte herself as witness in her own trial.

On Tuesday, the prosecution was supposed to present Police Major Jovelyn Magay, former Department of Education (DepEd) Assistant Secretary Sunshine Fajarda, and Commission on Audit- Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO) Assistant Commissioner and Chief Executive Staff Bresilio Sabaldan.
Presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero then asked Kapunan if the prosecution would already rest on Article 1.

“We will be resting on this article, You Honor, with the reservation of calling two possible witnesses at the end---the Vice President herself and perhaps an amicus curiae to aide this Honorable Court on understanding the intent of the drafters of the Constitution on Articles of Impeachment, on public officers, and public accountability,” Kapunan answered.
She said this will be done at the end, once all the Articles of Impeachment are presented by the prosecution.
“To summarize, there will be no more hearings, trials, on Article 1 on misuse and misappropriations of confidential funds,” the private prosecutor said.
Escudero, for the impeachment court’s part, advised the prosecution not to rest yet on Article 1, until it is decided whether or not additional witnesses will be called.
On Monday, the prosecution said they will present in advance Article 2 of the impeachment case, which refers to the alleged unexplained wealth of the Vice President.

House lead prosecutor and Batangas Representative Gerville Luistro, however, emphasized that the prosecution is not waiving the presentation of evidence for the bribery charge under Article 3 of the impeachment case. — RSJ, GMA News
