articles.title: End parliamentary courtesy for OP, OVP budgets – watchdogs
articles.summary: Lawmakers should stop giving the Office of the President and Office of the Vice President a free pass during budget deliberations and subject their spending plans to the same scrutiny as other…

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 12:00am

Calls to end the practice of extending “parliamentary courtesy” in the House and Senate come amid concerns over the size of allocations and alleged anomalies involving confidential and intelligence funds (CIF) and the Local Government Support Fund.
Philstar.com / Enrico Alonzo

MANILA, Philippines — Lawmakers should stop giving the Office of the President (OP) and Office of the Vice President (OVP) a free pass during budget deliberations and subject their spending plans to the same scrutiny as other agencies, according to budget watchdogs.
Public finance specialist Zy-za Nadine Suzara said this must be abolished as it undermines full budget transparency and accountability.

“Public trust is now very low because of opacity in the many aspects of the budget. It is no longer acceptable to accept parliamentary courtesy for both the OP and OVP in light of both the level of allocations and anomalies surrounding the use of the confidential and intelligence funds,” Suzara told The STAR.

Her remarks came after the House appropriations committee last week swiftly approved the OP’s proposed P10.2-billion budget for 2027, with lawmakers voting 37-5 to end the deliberations after invoking parliamentary courtesy.
The proposed allocation is about 64 percent lower than the OP’s P28-billion budget for 2026.
But Suzara said the OP’s proposed CIF accounts for about half of the total CIF being sought under the 2027 National Expenditure Program.

“On the other hand, the Vice President is on trial for the misuse of her confidential funds. Furthermore, the public deserves to know what other items are funded in the budgets of OP and OVP,” she added.
The OVP proposed a P785.2-million budget for next year, down 11.7 percent from its P889.24-million 2026 allocation.
For University of the Philippines professor and former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno, extending parliamentary courtesy to the OP and OVP is “inappropriate.”

“The funds allocated to the OP and OVP are not entitlements. They are public funds. Like any other office, they should account and explain how they are utilizing the people’s money and what are the outcomes and impacts they achieved in utilizing public fund. They should also explain the purpose of the funds they are requesting,” she said.
Legislative oversight over budget should not exempt any agency, particularly the OP and OVP, according to Tim Salomon of the Caucus of Development Non-Government Organizations Network.
“There should be no sacred cows in legislative oversight of the budget,” he said.

articles.title: Gas, diesel prices to hit P100/liter
articles.summary: Hefty pump adjustments are set to push gasoline and diesel prices above P100 per liter at some fuel stations today.

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 12:00am
Gasoline, diesel and kerosene prices will rise by as much as P4.69, P5.18 and P5.58 per liter, respectively, according to Energy Secretary Sharon Garin.
Rattanakun Thongbun via Canva Pro
MANILA, Philippines — Hefty pump adjustments are set to push gasoline and diesel prices above P100 per liter at some fuel stations today.
“We have an oil price hike, driven largely by higher international oil prices following renewed tensions affecting energy flows through the Middle East,” Garin said yesterday.
The weakening of the peso against the dollar also added pressure on domestic pump prices, with the local currency hitting record lows last week.
With the latest increases, gasoline prices in Metro Manila will reach as high as P102.04 per liter, while premium diesel will cost as much as P102.68 per liter.
Kerosene prices will range from P100.88 to P136.10 per liter.
Amid the ongoing energy emergency, the Department of Energy (DOE) is authorized to mandate the maximum price hikes and minimum rollbacks that oil firms can implement.
Rino Abad, director of the DOE’s Oil Industry Management Bureau, said domestic pump prices remain elevated as the geopolitical tensions continue to weigh on international supply chains.

Despite the absence of active peace talks, Abad still does not expect prices to immediately return to the peak levels seen during the height of the Middle East war, when prices climbed above P150 per liter.
While global supply flows have yet to normalize, the DOE reassured the public that the country’s fuel stockpiles continue to be sufficient and above the minimum required levels.
Fuel subsidy
Meanwhile, DOE officials said the government’s fuel subsidy program for public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers remains in effect this month, with funding averaging around P60 million per week.
Under the program, PUV and UV Express drivers will receive a P12-per-liter fuel discount, amounting to as much as P1,800 in weekly savings.

articles.title: Belugas transferred from Niagara Falls are under round-the-clock monitoring after deaths: Chicago aquarium
articles.summary: A Chicago aquarium says several of the belugas that were transferred to its site from Ontario's Marineland have health issues.

image.caption: A group of experts from Marineland and U.S. aquariums prepares to transport beluga whales onto a truck via a sling at Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Carlos Osorio/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New
A Chicago aquarium says several of the belugas that were transferred to its site from Ontario's Marineland have health issues.
Shedd Aquarium says it is monitoring whales' hydration

Shedd Aquarium said in a Friday statement it is conducting round-the-clock supervision, and teams are monitoring the whales' hydration, breathing rates, swim patterns, social interaction and other behaviors.

The aquarium's update comes after it reported last week that two of the three whales that died at its site in a week's span were belugas from Marineland, a theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., that closed after it ran out of money.
Shedd has said that Peekachu, one of the Marineland belugas, died on Aug. 25 at its site, two weeks after being relocated.
A 20-year-old beluga named Rain, which was moved from Marineland to the Chicago park in mid-August, also died, as well as a 34-year-old beluga that had lived for decades in Chicago.

items: Another beluga whale sent from Marineland to Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has died
'I tried to say goodbye and tried to tell him I love him': Canada's last captive whales leave Marineland

blocks.text: The Shedd Aquarium said there is still uncertainty surrounding the health of the remaining animals, and it is awaiting lab results as the park investigates the deaths.
"Some of the rescued belugas are showing more encouraging signs than others, but several have presented clinical concerns," Shedd wrote in the statement Friday.
"Their condition can change from day to day and, at times, hour to hour."
The aquarium said belugas get most of their hydration through the fish they eat, and while some of the rescued whales are eating regularly, others are not.
As a whole, Shedd said, none of the belugas are "where we want them to be from a health standpoint."
The Marineland belugas were given a clean bill of health in the days before their relocations, with Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson responsible for giving the final approval.

Marineland, which is now up for sale, completed the largest collective move of captive whales the world has ever seen last week, shipping 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in the United States and Spain over several weeks.
Marineland threatened to euthanize belugas
The final move last week brought an end to whale captivity in Canada.
Before their transfers, Marineland threatened to euthanize them if it did not get an emergency cash infusion after the federal government blocked an earlier plan to move the whales to China.
The whales would have been euthanized if they couldn't be moved to new homes, said the park's adviser, Andrew Burns.
"We were out of money, out of time," he said, adding it's "unbelievable" that Marineland pulled off the complex operation.
Multiple whales have died after being relocated.
In 2021, Marineland moved five whales to Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut.

Two of those whales died within a year of the move, and a third died two years after the transfer. Mystic said the whales had pre-existing conditions while Marineland said they were healthy when they left.
Nineteen belugas, one killer whale and one dolphin died at Marineland between 2019 and 2025.

articles.title: Europe’s centre fears nationalist wave after far-right AfD wins state in Germany
articles.summary: ‘Historic’ win in Saxony-Anhalt may show voters’ discontent with political centre, but sweeping conclusions cannot yet be drawn

blocks.text: The numbers speak for themselves: Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), a party that dabbles in Nazi imagery, distinguishes between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and is too extreme even for France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, nearly doubled its score in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt to 43.8% of the vote.

Meanwhile, the centre-right CDU of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, collapsed to 17.2%, less than half its total in the same race five years ago, and the centre-left SPD – Germany’s other main party of government for the past 60-odd years – scraped 9.3%. The least that can be said is that the centre did not hold.

It is not yet clear whether the AfD, whose local branch in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as “confirmed rightwing extremist”, will be able to form a government: it has 39 lawmakers in the 83-member parliament, just short of an outright majority.

But the score is the party’s strongest-ever state result and puts it closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since the second world war. It has sent shock waves round Europe, with nationalists cheering a “historic win” that is “just the beginning” and mainstream leaders warning of a “grave moment” for Europe.

Sweden holds legislative elections next weekend. France faces a crunch presidential ballot next spring. Key parliamentary races will follow there, as well as in Italy, Spain and Poland, later in the year. Far-right parties are polling strongly in all of them, and Europe’s centre fears a continent-wide nationalist wave.

It would be wise not to read too much into one election result in one quite particular German state. Saxony-Anhalt, analysts note, is home to barely 1.8 million voters and has long been a far-right stronghold: in federal and state elections over the past decade, support for the AfD there has consistently been double the national average.

“A far-right party winning a regional election in Germany is not more scary than a far-right party winning a regional election in France, the UK or the Netherlands,” said Tarik Abou-Chadi, a professor of European politics at Oxford University. “Saxony-Anhalt should not be the basis for sweeping conclusions about the electoral sociology of the AfD.”

Nonetheless, the AfD leads in national polls. It is also ahead – although in a far tighter race, with the SPD – in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where state elections are due later this month, and it is lying second even in liberal Berlin. Its rise is part of a decade-long march by far-right parties across Europe.

blocks.caption: The AfD is polling second even in liberal Berlin, and leading polls nationwide.  Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA

blocks.text: Almost one in four voters in Europe now cast their ballot for far-right parties, according to research led by Matthijs Rooduijn, a political scientist at the University of Amsterdam, a proportion that has grown nearly fivefold since the mid-1990s and climbed particularly steeply over the past three years.

This analysis, by more than 150 political scientists in 31 countries, found that the proportion of Europeans voting for a far-right party in their country’s most recent national elections had risen in 2026 to more than 23%, from about 10% a decade ago and roughly 5% in 1995.

Far-right populist parties are now in government as part of ruling coalitions in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, propping up a rightwing minority government in Sweden, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany (and, until very recently, the UK).

They have also suffered recent defeats, including in the Netherlands, where Geert Wilders’s Freedom party (PVV) lost nearly a third of its seats to finish second last year, and Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz was comprehensively beaten by his centre-right rival in April.
after newsletter promotion

But the trend seems clear. As Cas Mudde of the University of Georgia, a leading expert on Europe’s far right, put it after Orbán’s defeat: “The far right is here to stay, and many of its parties are as established as the (former) ‘mainstream’ parties. Like other parties, their electoral support fluctuates.”

That steady electoral advance has been achieved despite a refusal by mainstream parties in countries such as France and Germany to collaborate with far-right parties, prompting some commentators to argue that the “cordon sanitaire” or “firewall” has now failed, or even been counterproductive.

By keeping the AfD out, they argue, Germany’s mainstream parties have actually boosted it: the party has been protected from the compromises and failures inherent in government. At the same time, the centre has been “hollowed-out”: forced into uncomfortable, unstable alliances that agree on and – vitally – accomplish little, further frustrating voters and driving support for the extremes.

“There’s a self-reinforcing political dynamic that feeds the AfD’s rise,” said Mujtaba Rahman, of the Eurasia Group risk consultancy. “The weaker the election results, the less common ground in the coalition, the fewer the policy results. The fewer results, the bigger the frustration in the electorate, the bigger the AfD’s share of the vote.”

Many political scientists, however, say blaming the firewall is an excuse, and data suggests far-right parties do not in any case get weaker when they are in government, but become stronger: one recent study of more than 1,300 different governments in 57 countries found far-right parties that entered government averaged a score six percentage points higher come the next election.

Besides the persistent inability of mainstream governments to deliver for disillusioned voters hit by a spiralling cost of living crisis, it is above all the gradual mainstreaming and normalisation of the far right’s ideas that has driven – and continues to drive – its steady advance, political scientists argue.

Research suggests voter attitudes towards core far-right themes such as immigration have not changed significantly over time, but have become much more significant in their voting decisions: normalisation by the media and by mainstream parties that readily embrace far-right framing have legitimised far-right views.

“The entire debate about whether the cordon sanitaire is ‘successful’ or contributes to strengthening the far right completely misses the point,” said Gabriela Greilinger, an Austrian-Hungarian political scientist. “Far-right politics and policies already constantly take centre stage, whether or not the far right is in power. There is no cordon around their ideas.”

articles.title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
articles.summary: The long-running claim alleges Grindr breached UK privacy laws by sharing data with third parties.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByLiv McMahon
Technology reporter
Grindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.
The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.
The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.
According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.
Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.
The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September.

"While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.
The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.
'Significant distress'
The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.
It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.

People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.
Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.
She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Grindr became a publicly-listed company in 2022, two years after it was taken over by new owners

blocks.text: Grindr became a publicly-listed company in 2022, two years after it was taken over by new owners
Two data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.
The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.
It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.
Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.
It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.
The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community".
"Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

articles.title: French winemakers forecast 30-year low harvest after severe drought and heat
articles.summary:
Estimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect quality

French vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report…

blocks.text: French vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report a 30-year low in wine production after the country’s hottest ever recorded summer, according to the agriculture ministry.
Initial estimates suggest winemakers will produce just under 34m hectolitres from this year’s harvest: a drop of 6% on last year, and 17% less than ‌the 2021-2025 average.

Agreste, the government’s farming food, forestry and fishing statistics body, said the drop was partly caused by a reduction in the number and size of vineyards, but mostly the result of extreme weather conditions.

“The summer was particularly hot and dry: soil drought has intensified throughout the country and heatwaves have caused localised sun scald, scorching, defoliation, and wilting of the grapes, reducing harvest volumes,” it reported.

blocks.caption: A grape picker gets to work at the Trois Terres vineyard in Octon, southern France earlier this month. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA

blocks.text: However, some winemakers say with grape harvests still being conducted it is too early to make credible predictions.

The disappointing forecast comes after an optimistic start to the year, with heavy spring rains that encouraged grape growth. “The hot and dry summer conditions meant a deterioration of the [harvest] forecast,” Agreste reported.

A series of heatwaves brought the highest summer temperatures recorded in France since records began in 1900, with averages of 24C in June, July and August. Almost half of the country recorded temperatures on or above 40C.

Among the worst hit wine regions is Champagne where the grape harvest, which started unusually early in mid August, is predicted to be almost half that of last year. The Jura region in the east was the next worst hit with an estimated 37% loss. This year’s Burgundy-Beaujolais region grape production was expected to be one-third down, Agreste reported.

Winemakers in Bordeaux and the Languedoc-Roussillon as well as those in the south-east and south-west reported higher harvests this year but all except the Savoie region were down on the 2021-2025 five-year average for production.
However, Cécile Mathiaud of the Burgundy wine producers association said she was surprised by the government’s disastrous figures for her region’s vineyards.

“We know we won’t have a full harvest this year, but we have no definite figures and there’s no suggestion the situation is a disaster,” Mathiaud said. “We have some vineyards that have reported not much this year and others where it has been higher than expected.”

blocks.caption: The harvest under way early in the morning at Trois Terres. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA

blocks.text: Some Burgundy vineyards began their harvest in early August but others are collecting the grapes now, she added. “Our reference is the historically low harvest of 2021 when we produced only 1m hectolitres; we think it will be higher this year, but the question is by how much? I have absolutely no idea how the ministry has come up with these figures.”
after newsletter promotion

Agreste said the figures were estimates and definitive results would not be known until regions made official harvest declarations later this year. It added that 2026 grape harvests were “marked by significant regional disparities”.

Wine harvests have traditionally taken place in France between September and mid October, but the climate emergency has brought dates forward slightly each year for the last four decades. This year, the harvest timetable advanced at least a week compared with last year throughout the country. Some vineyards in Bordeaux began two weeks early.

There are also concerns that vines and grapes in some of France’s best-known wine producing regions, including Bordeaux, have been damaged by smoke from rampant wildfires. No major Bordeaux vineyards suffered direct damage from the flames that came within 15km (9 miles) of the city, but there is concern that smoke has entered the grape skins causing “smoke taint” and affecting the taste of the finished wine.

The agriculture ministry would normally issue harvest estimates in early August, but postponed its analysis at the request of the wine industry because of what it described as “the high level of uncertainty surrounding these forecasts” caused by weather conditions and wildfires.
France’s wine sector is already under pressure owing to a decline in demand. Annual wine consumption in the 1960s in France was 127 litres each year compared with 40 litres a year now.
Wine drinking in the US, France’s largest export market, has also dropped and French wines have been hit by Donald Trump’s tariffs.

articles.title: Remulla to visit France amid Zaldy Co and Loren Legarda’s stay
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday said he will visit France to coordinate with authorities after Sen. Loren Legarda and former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co stayed there amid…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday said he will visit France to coordinate with authorities after Sen. Loren Legarda and former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co stayed there amid their cases here.
Legarda is facing a plunder complaint before the Ombudsman while Co is subject of two malversation cases now handled by the Sandiganbayan.
“I will go to France in the coming days to talk to French authorities, because France should not be a safe haven for plunderers and ill-gotten wealth,” Remulla said in a press conference in Filipino.
“Because Zaldy Co is there. Loren Legarda is there. So this is becoming a trend that, maybe, the country is being used as a hideout. We will make their world smaller,” he also said.

Co faces two counts of malversation over an alleged non-existent P77 million worth of flood control project in Bulacan and road dike project in Oriental Mindoro worth P289.4 million, which prosecutors said was found with structural deficiencies.

Legarda, along with her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, was accused by prosecutors of “conspiring to secure exclusive government rights over the country’s solar energy resources through legislative and regulatory actions,” resulting in more than P10.44 billion in unpaid financial obligations to the government.
Legarda, who first filed her medical leave on Aug. 3, extended her leave for the fifth time until Sept. 16.
Co, Legarda, and Leviste have repeatedly denied the allegations.
Remulla said he has no information if both Co and Legarda have already applied for asylum in France.

“I have no information, but that is (seeking asylum) now in the offing … but if they saw that they would have a reputation of being a hideout for ill-gotten wealth, I think the people there will also refuse them,” Remulla said. /cb

articles.title: War criminal Ratko Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade, Serbia
articles.summary: Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb commander convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, has been buried in Belgrade. The funeral, broadcast live on TV, comes just days before President Vucic is expected…

image.caption: Former Bosnian Serb army commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on MondayImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: Several thousand people lined the streets of Belgrade on Monday to follow the funeral service and burial of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic.

Earlier in the day, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije personally officiated at the funeral service for the former general, who died while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide in Srebrenica and other war crimes committed during the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In accordance with his wishes, Mladic was laid to rest at Topcider Cemetery beside his daughter, who died by suicide in 1994.

Informer TV, a staunchly pro-government broadcaster, carried live coverage of what it described as a "magnificent farewell," without mentioning the roughly 8,000 Bosniak civilians and prisoners massacred by Mladic's Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica in July 1995.
President Vucic not in attendance
President Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral, citing a previously scheduled visit by his counterpart from Uzbekistan.
Observers say that the president has tried to chart a middle course on the issue of Mladic's funeral.

blocks.caption: Thousands gathered in the Serbian capital to witness Mladic's funeral procession Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mladic was not buried with state honors, but with military honors, with Vucic insisting that the state was merely respecting the wishes of the family and ensuring a dignified burial.
"Were we supposed to forbid people from attending, forbid the funeral itself and create dog cemeteries?" he said in response to criticism from the EU.
The phrase "dog cemeteries" refers in Serbia to the unmarked graves of so-called "enemies of the people" who were executed by Yugoslav partisans during and immediately after World War II.

Vucic was equally dismissive of the decision by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos to cancel a planned visit to Belgrade, calling her reaction "stupid." He has brushed aside other criticism of the public glorification of Mladic in much the same way.

An EU spokesman said in a statement that "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."
Politically tricky time for Vucic
For Vucic, who has long sought to balance Serbia between the European Union and Russia, the situation is politically delicate.
He is expected to call a snap parliamentary election as early as this week. The poll is likely to take place on October 25.

blocks.caption: Mladic was buried with military honorsImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: For the first time in years, there is a credible possibility that his ruling bloc could be defeated by the student movement, which has led anti-government protests in Serbia for nearly two years now.
Vucic is expected to head the list of his Serbian Progressive Party as its candidate for prime minister.
Elections also in Bosnia and Hercegovina
According to Dejan Bursac, a political scientist at the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory in Belgrade, all signs point to a president increasingly anxious about the upcoming vote.

"Vucic is grasping at every available lifeline," Bursac told DW. "One of those lifelines is Mladic's funeral and the nationalism it can help generate, allowing Vucic to present himself as a patriot while portraying his political opponents as traitors."

Many Serbs, Bursac said, still feel deep resentment over the outcome of the Yugoslav wars and claim that crimes committed against Serbs during these wars largely went unpunished. "That sentiment is now being deliberately inflamed and politically exploited," said Bursac.

blocks.caption: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has brushed aside criticism from the European UnionImage: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka in the predominantly Serb entity of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Srebrenica is located, sees a similar dynamic.
"Politics here rests heavily on emotion," she told DW. "This is an issue around which citizens are mobilized. They forget how difficult their lives are because patriotic fervor takes over."
Bosnia and Herzegovina will go to the polls before Serbia, with elections there scheduled for October 4.
Students have a different focus

In Serbia, the student movement — a coalition of faculty assemblies and protest groups operating without formal leaders or public representatives — has largely avoided commenting on Mladic, the funeral or wartime crimes on its social media channels.

Analysts note that both Vucic's party and the student-backed electoral list, which is expected to include respected professors, activists and other public figures, are attempting to function as broad "catch-all" political platforms.
In Serbia, that means neither side can afford to alienate nationalistically minded voters. "Especially because the election will most likely be decided by a very narrow margin," said Dejan Bursac.
The students, he argued, have recognized that for many citizens, it is enough to campaign for the rule of law, democracy and against systemic corruption.

blocks.caption: The student movement, which has been leading anti-government protests in Serbia for almost two years, has largely avoided commenting on Mladic or arrangements for his funeral. Pictured here: people at a protest rally in JuneImage: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW

blocks.text: The protest movement began with university blockades after the collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, in November 2024. Sixteen people were killed.
Although prosecutors have opened several investigations, including into possible corruption linked to construction contracts, no trial has yet begun.
The power of media control
Few people in Serbia place much faith in opinion polls. Nevertheless, it is widely assumed that both the ruling party and the student movement command roughly 40% support each.
The government directly or indirectly controls most television stations and major news outlets, many of which frequently publish identical content.
In recent days, pro-Vucic tabloid Informer has targeted anyone who describes Mladic as a war criminal, branding such critics as "professional haters of Serbs" and "traitors."

Yet political narratives in Serbia shift quickly. Vucic alone appeared on television roughly 400 times last year. By the time voters head to the polls in late October, he will almost certainly need a new issue to rally supporters around.
Mladic's funeral is unlikely to carry him all the way to election day.

articles.title: Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'
articles.summary: A visibly shaken but also determined Friedrich Merz spoke in Berlin about the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt and the CDU's bitter defeat. He insisted on sticking to his reforms.

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Saxony-Anhalt's Premier Sven Schulze spoke about the impact of the electionImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are situations in which politicians who have little left to say to each other still appear together before the press. This was certainly the case when Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) and his party colleague, Sven Schulze, the state premier of Saxony-Anhalt, discussed the results of Sunday's state election. They described the results as a catastrophe for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — an earthquake, a disaster. Merz appeared shaken and devastated, to put it mildly.

He thanked Schulze for his work during the campaign. Then Merz added: "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany. It will have repercussions, including on the international stage."

This is because the victors in the state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), oppose supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia's war of aggression, and many AfD politicians maintain close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin's government, Merz explained.
No regard for the rule of law?
Speaking about the AfD, Merz adopted an almost confrontational tone. Majorities can change, he said, and democrats must always be aware of that and accept it.

But, Merz said, it is shocking that 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that disregard the rule of law in Germany. Merz was talking about not only the AfD but also the socialist Left Party and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which split off from the Left Party over issues that align the BSW with the AfD.

In contrast, the chancellor said his government will always defend the values of the German constitution: "In our country, these values are not up for debate. Power is granted, not seized. And the minority is not the enemy of the majority."
Historians have long described the Nazis' rise to power in the German Reich as a "seizure of power," which is why Merz's statement is sure to be the subject of much discussion.

Seeking to reassure Germany's international partners in the EU and NATO, he said, "We know that Germany bears a special responsibility because of its history. We will always defend our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe."
What the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt win means for Germany
Could CDU politicians in Saxony-Anhalt help the AfD come to power?

Standing next to him, Schulze remained silent. On election night the previous evening, long after his defeat had become clear, Schulze repeatedly emphasized in numerous statements that the public's widespread dissatisfaction with the Merz government in Berlin had dealt him a massive blow.
As for now, the worst-case scenario has narrowly been averted: the AfD does not have an absolute majority in the Magdeburg state parliament — but only by the narrowest of margins.

And this is a problem for Friedrich Merz: Dissatisfaction is growing, even within his own ranks. Can he prevent individual CDU lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt from voting — against the official party line — to elect Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD election winner, as head of government?
If not, then both of Merz's seats of power would be in serious jeopardy: his position as chairman of the party and his seat in the Chancellery.
Merz defends his controversial reforms

However, as of today, Merz is still defending the difficult reforms his government has undertaken. One such reform is the overhaul of the chronically deficit-ridden pension system, which will bring great hardship to many people in Germany and faced fierce opposition during the election campaign.

On election night, Vice Chancellor and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leader Lars Klingbeil suggested reassessing the reforms following the defeat of the coalition government in Berlin. However, Merz has not mentioned such a change in course.
How the AfD changed its pitch and broke through
AfD displays confidence

Hours before the chancellor's appearance at the CDU headquarters, the AfD took to the stage at the Federal Press Conference. The top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, sarcastically thanked the media, which had largely portrayed him during the campaign as a threat to democracy and the rule of law.
"It was also thanks to you that we made it," Siegmund said, adding, "Thank you very much for the great coverage during this election campaign."
For example, the influential news magazine Der Spiegel had recently labeled the AfD politician "Germany's most dangerous man" in a widely circulated cover story.

Siegmund then looked out triumphantly at the packed hall and declared, "Never before has there been such a wide gap between those members of the media who seek to dictate to us here in Saxony-Anhalt how we should live and the reality of life for the people in this state."

But Siegmund avoided the question about whether the election result is a clear mandate for his party to form a government — even one without a majority of its own, if necessary, or possibly with the tacit support of the economically left, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

Siegmund, however, has said he does not want to be a partner in a coalition — he wants absolute power, and he doesn't have it. The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will surely be the subject of much discussion for many days, perhaps even weeks, to come.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of 'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
articles.summary: Mladić was jailed for genocide during the 1990s Bosnian war and the EU warned Serbia not to glorify the convicted war criminal.

blocks.text: Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.
Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.

He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.

A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral ​but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification".
Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.

During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people.
Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation.
Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils.

Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported.

The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him".

Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on.
Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine.
Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.
In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags.
Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.
On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade.
For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war.

A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade.
Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said.
"He should be remembered only as a butcher."

Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail.

The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors."
Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said.
"It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past."

blocks.text: The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg.
The German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease its operations by September 18 the latest, according to Russia's Foreign Ministry.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences.
The move is a direct response to Germany's closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin.

Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport. Russia has called the idea that it is behind the attack an absurd fabrication.

articles.title: Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms
articles.summary:
US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns”…

blocks.text: The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.

In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.
It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.

The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.

Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.

In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.

“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.

“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”

The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.

A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”
Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.
Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.

The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.
Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.
Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.
Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.
“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”
Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.

However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.

articles.title: Federal investigators search for cause of Amazon cargo jet crash that killed five
articles.summary:
Theories begin to emerge that plane may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time

Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what…

blocks.text: Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what caused an Amazon cargo jet to barrel off a runway at Miami international airport on Sunday afternoon and crash, killing five people and injuring five others.

Video footage showed the jet wobbling a little and coming in fast and far along the runway, with storm clouds clearly visible in the sky behind, as expert theories began to emerge that the Boeing 767 may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time.

The aircraft overshot the runway around 2pm Sunday after arriving in south Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a perimeter road used by warehouse workers and other businesses before coming to rest in a parking lot. With its nose tipped forward, flames then burst out of part of the jet and thick, dark smoke began billowing into the air.
Authorities have not named the five who died or the five people injured, three critically, or released exact details on where the casualties were located.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said chairwoman Jennifer Homendy would hold a news conference later on Monday. US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said on social media that the agency would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”.

The crash trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah said. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
Jadallah described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.

Video of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-33A, operated by contractor 21 Air, posted to social media show it touching down far along the runway. Other footage shows the plane with a left hand wheel on the landing gear still a little above the ground as the jet speeds down the tarmac, apparently abnormally fast, and then overruns the end of the runway, where the right undercarriage collapsed and the wing caught fire.

Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 ft (914 meters) of a runway. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should normally have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the transportation department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
Storm clouds can be seen in the area and strong winds reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.

Miami airport is not equipped with “arresting beds”, systems of lightweight, crushable material that the federal aviation authority (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide at the end of runways to help safely stop planes that overshoot.
Some 200 emergency personnel responded to the incident, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the fire department said.

The flight operators, 21 Air, is a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando international airport, more than 200 miles north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there. Flights later resumed, although two runways at the busy airport remained out of service on Monday morning.

Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement on Sunday: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. And Amazon said in a further statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

items: The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Song Yadong eyes history for China in UFC after home victory
articles.summary: UFC fighter Song Yadong smiled as he recalled the roaring crowds at his latest win in Shanghai that brought him one step closer to his goal of becoming China’s first male champion. On home…

blocks.text: Chinaís Song Yadong celebrates after winning against Russia’s Umar Nurmagomedov in their menís bantamweight fight during the UFC Fight Night at Oriental Sports Center in Shanghai on August 29, 2026. (Photo by Jade Gao / AFP)
UFC fighter Song Yadong smiled as he recalled the roaring crowds at his latest win in Shanghai that brought him one step closer to his goal of becoming China’s first male champion.
On home turf, Song’s second-round knockout against Russian fighter Umar Nurmagomedov last week put him third in UFC Bantamweight rankings.
“I was actually really shocked,” the 28-year-old told AFP at China’s UFC Performance Institute.
“In the arena, the sound of the cheering was really loud. But that was probably the happiest moment of my life.”
Song said he was “just a kid” with a dream of making it in the UFC when he debuted in Shanghai in 2017.
“When I suddenly made it there, I realised it was full of top-tier fighters. If I wanted to stay there, I knew I’d have to train constantly to improve myself,” he said.
Nine years later, Song knocked out Nurmagomedov in the bantamweight category in Pudong’s Oriental Sports Center.
Song, who gave himself the nickname “Kung Fu Kid,” first became fascinated with UFC as a teenager watching highlight reels of the sport online.
He references his roots in his entrance music, which is the theme song for “Journey to the West,” a popular Chinese TV show based on a Ming-era story.
As a child, Song said, he would turn on the TV and play the theme song on repeat.
The music in the show played when Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, jumped out.
“I felt like I was just like him, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and I wanted my entrance to be just like his,” Song said.
UFC continues to build its audience in Asia, and this summer’s Fight Night in Shanghai saw a record crowd for the region, with over 16,000 fans in attendance.
Zhang Weili, a female UFC fighter, became the face of the sport in China after winning the belt twice.
Song said his victory last week was just a stepping stone.
“This isn’t the end,” he said as he aims to become the World Champion in his weight class.
“I believe I’m very close to making it a reality.”

articles.title: Carbon capture tech exists. Scaling it up is the hard part
articles.summary: Europe just opened a carbon capture and storage plant billed as the continent's largest. But global climate scenarios call for far more capacity than exists anywhere on Earth.

image.caption: CCS targets point sources, like at this coal plant: a single smokestack where CO2 can be captured before it disperses into the atmosphereImage: Florian Gaertner/photothek/IMAGO

blocks.text: For years there has been talk of capturing and storing the carbon dioxide generated by burning fossil fuels as one way to keep the planet from overheating. In fact, the United Nations' climate science body envisions somewhere between 350 to 1,200 gigatons of CO2 storage within the century to avoid the worst effects of climate change.
But is it really happening? Yes and no.

Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, is an effort to trap CO2 at what's called a point source. This might be a smokestack or at an ammonia factory — in other words, a single, concentrated spot where the planet-heating greenhouse gas is emitted.
After being captured, it is compressed and transported, usually using pipelines or trains, before being stored geologically — in aquifers or old oil reservoirs, for example.

CCS is related to, but distinct from, carbon dioxide removal (CDR), which involves pulling CO2 out of the atmosphere after it's already been emitted. That CO2 is often stored similarly to CCS, but uses very different technologies for capturing.

"Given the legacy of emissions in the atmosphere, given where we are in terms of emissions reductions, we're going to need these approaches," said Wil Burns, co-director of the Institute for Carbon Removal Law & Policy at American University.
"We just have to figure out how to use them thoughtfully and still keep our eye on the prize of decarbonizing."
The technology works, but scaling is another matter
The feasibility of CCS and CDR is a subject of much debate among scientists and climate campaigners.
Advocates for scaling up the technology as a key pillar of decarbonization say the main hurdle is getting more plants built, which would require government subsidies and policy intervention.

Without governments putting a price on carbon or offering tax credits, experts say it's hard to imagine investors shelling out for these expensive commercial projects. Renewable energy, by contrast, has become so cheap over time that it's often commercially viable on its own.
"It's ready to go, technologically. We know how to do this process," said Susan Hovorka, a geoscientist at the University of Texas-Austin, researching CCS since 1998.
Carbon capture: Is it feasible?
How CCS began

CCS traces its roots back to the 1960s, when oil companies began piping natural CO2 into oil fields for enhanced oil recovery — that's where captured CO2 is injected into old oil fields to help push more oil out of the ground. It wasn't until 1996 that the first large-scale CCS project designed to reduce emissions went online in Norway.
Progress since then has been slowly ramping up. In 2020, there were 26 operational commercial CCS facilities around the world. As of last summer, the number has nearly tripled.
But others say the technology remains in its infancy, and our real-world capabilities lag far behind our technical knowhow.

"What is not well-established and basically doesn't exist at scale is the commercial experience doing this," said Danny Cullenward, an economist at the University of Pennsylvania's Kleinman Center for Energy Policy. "And proving that it works; that it's easy, that it's cost-effective, that it can be deployed at large scale, that it works in lots of different places."

Researchers from the University of Texas-Austin recently revealedthat though small-scale pilot projects have been successful in injecting CO2 into the ground, many of the world's large-scale CCS initiatives are pumping far less into storage sites than promised.

And they are not unlimited. While previous estimates put the Earth's CO2 storage capacity somewhere between 10,000 and 40,000 gigatons, a new study foundthe number is just about 1,460 gigatons, meaning most CCS-reliant climate scenarios would breach the planetary limit for storage over the next 250 years.

blocks.caption: Visitors walk through the Northern Lights facility in Norway, where captured CO2 is compressed and prepared for injection thousands of meters beneath the seabedImage: Benoit Doppagne/BELGA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Climate models bet heavy on new technology

Starting this week, the European fertilizer giant Yara will open what it calls Europe's largest carbon capture project. It will harvest excess CO2 at its factory in Sluiskil Netherlands, liquefy it, and ship it to Norway's Atlantic coast to be stored in an underground rock formation, some 2,600 meters below the seabed.

That plant will only be able to capture 800,000 metric tons of CO2 annually. To meet that 350 gigaton threshold — the lower end of the UN's climate scenarios used to inform climate policy — would require about 5,800 more Yara-size plants to open tomorrow.

The International Energy Agency, another intergovernmental body that models climate data, projected7.6 gigatons of carbon will be captured every year by 2050, with almost all of it stored. Right now, the world's 77 operating plants are capable of capturing 64 million tons annually. That output would need to be multiplied by 119 over the next quarter-century to reach the IEA number.
"The scale of what's being called for in those scenarios is astronomically beyond any real activity that exists today," Cullenward said.
He says climate models tend to underestimate renewables and lean too hard on "gee-whiz" technologies.

That's because models basically have three ways to hit an ambitious climate target: add more renewables, use less energy, or bet on some new technology that solves the problem without forcing society to change much.
"If you tell a model to solve an impossible problem, it's like pouring water down a flight of stairs — it's going to find the fastest way to get to the bottom," Cullenward said.

blocks.caption: CO2 tanks at the Northern Lights storage facility where captured carbon — including from Yara's Sluiskil plant — is liquefied before being injected into a rock formation deep beneath the seabedImage: Alessandro Della Valle/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: A license to keep drilling?

One of the most contentious arguments about CCS is whether it represents a legitimate decarbonization solution or is a tactic from oil and gas companies to justify and prolong more fossil fuel extraction.

In 2023, about 80% of the world's CCS capacity was used for enhanced oil recovery, according to research and advocacy group, Oil Change International — ultimately increasing emissions and defeating CCS's climate benefit.
Some researchers also argue that CCS poses a moral hazard, or a situation where having a form of protection allows for more risk-taking.
On the other hand, advocates for the technology often talk of reserving CCS for what's called "hard-to-abate" industries, like cement.

"I don't think we're going to get to five or 10 or 20 gigatons a year of carbon removal," Cullenward said. "But we may need to get as much as we can and to me that's a reason to be more engaged rather than less engaged."
Why carbon capture needs a reality check
