articles.title: Tyson Fury claims Anthony Joshua bout is off, calls for Usyk trilogy
articles.summary: Tyson Fury claims Anthony Joshua is backing out of their much-anticipated all-British heavyweight showdown and has challenged Oleksandr Usyk to a trilogy fight. Fury and Joshua have been locked in…

blocks.text: FILE – Tyson Fury of England celebrates after winning against Mariusz Wach of Poland during a heavyweight charity bout at Max Muay Thai Stadium in Pattaya, Thailand, Friday, July 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Sakchai Lalit, file)
Tyson Fury claims Anthony Joshua is backing out of their much-anticipated all-British heavyweight showdown and has challenged Oleksandr Usyk to a trilogy fight.
Fury and Joshua have been locked in talks over a long-awaited meeting but the “Gypsy King” is impatient at a lack of confirmation, calling his rival a “coward” last week.
The two former heavyweight world champions are expected to meet in November but the location of the fight has yet to be agreed.
In an expletive-laden video posted on Instagram, Fury, 38, claimed Joshua was pulling out of the fight.

“This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk,” he said. “Oleksandr you’re his (Joshua’s) trainer and his sensei and you know he is… weak-minded… and that he would never fight the Gypsy King, which you have had the guts to do twice.
“You got the decisions last time, fair play to you. Good luck to you, let’s do it again. Let’s run it back in November.
“The ball is now in your court… do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling quits? Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent.”
Fury has twice lost to Usyk, a two-time undisputed heavyweight champion.
Joshua has been working with the Ukrainian’s training team.
New York’s Madison Square Garden was widely expected to be announced as the venue for the Fury-Joshua fight even though Joshua’s camp prefers Wembley Stadium.
Sela, the Saudi state-owned promotional company financing the fight, and broadcaster Netflix are believed to favour staging the bout in the United States.

articles.title: Why is far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?
articles.summary: Aftershocks of party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt will ripple across Germany, with two more state elections this month

blocks.text: Germany is reeling from the biggest far-right victory in a state election since the Nazi period after voters in Saxony-Anhalt in the former communist east gave the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party a thumping first-place finish of 44%, just short of an absolute majority.

blocks.caption: Alice Weidel (right, with Ulrich Siegmund, centre, and her AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, left) said the AfD was targeting a 40% vote at the next general election. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA

blocks.text: What happened and why is it significant?

For the first time since the second world war, a German state is on the brink of electing a far-right government after a big win in Saxony-Anhalt, described by the news magazine Der Spiegel as a magnitude 9.0 “political earthquake”.

Coming in nearly 27 points ahead of the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), the conservative party of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, the AfD pulled off a coup whose aftershocks will ripple across Germany and beyond its borders. The AfD will have broad powers over education, culture and ‌domestic security if it manages to take power in the state. Among other policies, it has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms. It now has a strong wind at its back for the two state elections yet to come this month.

Its triumph also raised doubts whether the unpopular Merz could hold on in the face of such a clear rejection of his policies and leadership after just 16 months in power. The AfD co-leader Alice Weidel told reporters in Berlin that her party was targeting a 40% result at the next general election, scheduled for 2029. It is currently polling in first place at 28%.
What might happen next?

The AfD’s national leaders and the chief candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, the media-savvy former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, said the state’s voters had given the party a clear mandate to govern. However, without an absolute majority in the state parliament, the party would need partners or supporters to either join a coalition or “tolerate” a minority government. Siegmund said repeatedly before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority. The remaining parties ruled out playing kingmaker to Siegmund by lending formal support. However, the BSW, a small “left-conservative” populist party which narrowly cleared the 5% hurdle to representation, has hinted at tacit cooperation.

Prior to the election, some Christian Democrats in the state openly questioned the “firewall” policy. Siegmund indicated he would spend the coming days and weeks “with an outstretched hand”, testing the hitherto resolute opposition to helping the AfD into power. If Siegmund fails to build a coalition, he suggested holding a new election, something that would require a two-thirds majority in the state legislature.
What does the result say about the firewall approach?

The stunning outcome in Saxony-Anhalt has underscored doubts about the viability of the policy of mainstream parties to exclude the AfD from power. The only other time the AfD won in a state, in neighbouring Thuringia in 2024, its victory was less decisive, allowing the remaining parties to cobble together an ideologically awkward, cross-spectrum coalition. Given the AfD’s margin of victory in Saxony-Anhalt, it is difficult to imagine how the humiliated CDU could form such a “Frankenstein” alliance of disparate parties this time. The state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged the party no longer had a mandate to try.

blocks.caption: Siegmund has suggested a new election if he fails to build a coalition. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA

blocks.text: What does the result mean for the CDU and Frederich Merz?

Sunday’s election amounted to a stinging rebuke of Merz and his CDU. The stony-faced chancellor admitted he was “deeply shocked” by the result. Exit polls showed voters were furious about his broken promises to revive the economy and shore up fiscal discipline. Energy prices, stoked by inflation and the Iran war, have hit voters hard in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany’s poorest state. Cost of living issues appeared to far outweigh immigration, the AfD’s trademark call to arms, as a mobilising issue. Although support for the AfD has been strongest in the ex-communist east, the party also made strong gains in two elections in western states earlier this year amid fears over deindustrialisation.

The Social Democratic party (SPD), a junior partner in Merz’s alliance, indicated on Monday it would be willing to water down planned changes to Germany’s costly and creaking social welfare system in order to placate disgruntled voters. Merz insisted the measures to shore up the healthcare and pension systems were necessary and vowed to remain and fight for them “in the interest of our children and grandchildren”.

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz has been ‘deeply shocked’ by the result.  Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA

blocks.text: What about the next two state elections?

Voters in the German capital, Berlin, and the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, two of Germany’s 16 länder, will go to the polls on 20 September. The obvious momentum for the AfD, as well as widespread German dissatisfaction with Merz and his right-left government with the SPD, mean those polls are also fraught with risk for the parties in the federal coalition. The AfD currently has a narrow lead ahead of the co-ruling SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but for now looks unlikely to win an absolute majority. The situation in Berlin – once divided between east and west – looks muddled, with the CDU, far-left Linke and the AfD all jockeying for first place. Even if the CDU managed to hold on to its lead on election day, it would struggle to form an ideologically coherent coalition, dealing Merz and his party another stinging blow that could further destabilise his government.

articles.title: Very strong El Niño to bring way below-normal rainfall in PH
articles.summary: MANILA – Most parts of the country will likely experience way below-normal rainfall as a very strong El Niño is expected to develop toward yearend, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and…

blocks.text: MANILA – Most parts of the country will likely experience way below-normal rainfall as a very strong El Niño is expected to develop toward yearend, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) chief said Monday.
“This means 60 percent or more reduction of average rainfall in a month,” PAGASA Administrator Nathaniel Servando told the Philippine News Agency in an interview.
A moderate to strong El Niño is present in the Tropical Pacific.
The ongoing El Niño is forecast to continue until the first half of 2027, and may reach a very strong state before the end of 2026.
For September, below normal rainfall will prevail over most of Northern Luzon, and near normal rainfall over the rest of the country.
By October, below normal rainfall conditions will prevail over Luzon, the Visayas, and Caraga, while near normal rainfall is likely over the rest of Mindanao.
Way below normal to below normal conditions are expected across the country in November. Patches of near normal rainfall are forecast in some areas in Mindanao.
For December, PAGASA forecasts above normal rainfall over most of Luzon and Western Visayas, while below normal rainfall will likely prevail over most of the Visayas and Mindanao.
Servando explained that the “above normal rainfall” in Luzon in December may not be significant since it is normally dry in Western Luzon.
“Normal rainfall in December is relatively low, and this might be due to the shearline or the northeast monsoon,” he said.
In January 2027, way below normal to below normal rainfall will prevail across the country, except for near normal rainfall conditions in some parts of Mindanao.
The whole country is expected to experience way below normal to below normal rainfall in February.
“The peak of El Niño will be from October to December, but impacts may vary depending on locations and the severity,” Servando added. (PNA)

articles.title: 'It's incredible,' Winnipeg man says after car blows over onto someone else's lawn in storm
articles.summary: A Winnipeg man says the damage left by Sunday night's thunderstorm was "overwhelming," after his vehicle rolled into the front yard of a nearby home.

image.caption: Darryl Gervais says winds during Sunday night's thunderstorm pushed his car so hard that it rolled over into a nearby lawn on Lindsay Street in Winnipeg's River Heights area. (Gavin Axelrod/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated
A Winnipeg man says the damage left by Sunday night's thunderstorm was "overwhelming," after his vehicle rolled into the front yard of a nearby home.
Some power outages for roughly 4,000 Hydro customers could stretch into Tuesday
High winds and heavy rains led to downed power lines and trees, particularly in Winnipeg's Westwood and River Heights areas, Hydro spokesperson Peter Chura told CBC News on Monday morning.
Sometime during the storm, Darryl Gervais says the wind pushed his Pontiac Vibe, which rolled over into a nearby lawn on Lindsay Street in the River Heights area.
Gervais said he had just finished repairs on the vehicle and left it for his son to use right before the storm hit.
"It looked wonderful, and now it doesn't," he told CBC News on Monday. "The windows are smashed, the roof is crumpled, and there's a trail of parts along the lawn."
But Gervais is glad no one was hurt, saying if the vehicle had rolled another three metres, it would have hit a house.
"It's incredible, the force of the wind that can pick up a 3,000 pound vehicle," he said.
"Yesterday, I was working on it, figuring it would last another two years."

Preliminary numbers from Environment Canada show winds in the city reached 83 kilometres per hour on Sunday night, while 35 millimetres of rain hit Winnipeg overall and The Forks got nearly 70 millimetres.
Robyn Canicula, who lives nearby on Lindsay Street, says her family may be staying in a hotel for the next few days, after the storm damaged her home just before her children head back to school.
"We can't go in the backyard because there's a power line down," Canicula told CBC News on Monday. "Our trampoline's gone, our pergola's up in a tree down the road."
The storm left destruction all over the neigbourhood, including downed power lines and trees, as well as power lines that were cut in half, she said.
"It feels like we're in a movie. It's pretty scary."
Canicula is thankful the community has come together in light of the damage, she said.

"We've had a lot of neighbors reach out," she said. "Actually, somebody's been helping my husband put a tarp on our roof and our neighbour's roof, so it's been really nice, all the support we've been getting from the community."

items: What's open and closed this Labour Day in Manitoba

blocks.text: About 4,000 customers in Winnipeg were without power on Monday morning, Hydro's Chura said.

Although crews worked through the night to repair damage and restore power to some, people in areas that suffered severe damage should expect "extended outages today and likely into tomorrow," Chura said.
"We'll assess the damage and concentrate on the damage that's going to restore the most customers to power at once, and then work our way down from there," he said.
"There's more severe weather in the forecast, so that could complicate repairs and cause further hazards for people."
Hydro is urging the public to stay away from downed powerlines and to report them to 911, said Chura.
"And remember, a downed tree can also be hiding other hazards, so stay away from those as well."
With files from Gavin Axelrod

articles.title: Nathan Fielder teases Elizabeth Holmes documentary with eyebrow-raising trailer
articles.summary: Fielder's new film about Holmes, You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.

image.caption: Nathan Fielder, creator and executive producer of the television series The Rehearsal, arrives at the 86th annual Peabody Awards on Sunday, May 31, 2026, at the Beverly Wilshire in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Fielder's new film about Holmes, You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.
Documentary centres on weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration following 2022 Theranos fraud conviction
If you were wondering what possible antics Nathan Fielder has been up to after watching the latest season of The Rehearsal, we have your answer.

The Vancouver-born comedian, writer and director released a teaser late Sunday for his next project, a documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes who was famously convicted of fraud in 2022 after her company claimed to have created a type of blood testing that could screen for hundreds of diseases with small amounts of blood.
Fielder's film, titled You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.
Oppenheim's previous works include Spermworld (2024), an FX-produced doc about sperm donors and Some Kind of Heaven (2020) about a Florida retirement community.

items: Theranos's Elizabeth Holmes sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison

blocks.text: Fielder grew to fame with Nathan For You, a series on Comedy Central in which he gives horrible business advice to entrepreneurs. Previously he won (and baffled) Canadian hearts and minds with his appearances on CBC's This Hour Has 22 Minutes, in field segments titled "Nathan On Your Side" in 2008 and 2009.
You Can See Everything is being distributed by Gen Z favourite A24. The trailer features the company's signature high-saturation colour grading and overall eeriness.

It includes a roughly-one minute close-up conversation between Holmes and Fielder. The two intensely gaze at each other, as Holmes says, "Why would I deceive you? There's no — there's no reason for me to do that."
A long-ish silence follows and Fielder — with an incredulous expression on his face — says, "You're being real right now?"

The trailer was released in conjunction with a surprise screening Sunday at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado. Reviews haven't yet surfaced from the screening, several critics posted their superlative-filled reactions to social media.

Film director Daniel Howat wrote on X after the screening that You Can See Everything "is maybe the most hysterical, shocking, insane documentary I’ve ever seen. Endlessly thought-provoking ... A work of genius."

Los Angeles-based music producer Erik Nordgren called it "easily the best film of the year for me, arguably on my best of the decade list. It turns from an uneasy-as-hell doc into something structurally, stylistically, and formally even more shocking. Like nothing I’ve ever seen."

The exchange harkens back to another uncomfortable, lesser-known interview Fielder conducted on This Hour Has 22 Minutes with former CBC president Hubert T. Lacroix in 2008. The two sit across from each other and Lacroix is put on the spot when he says he's a fan of Fielder's work but struggles to come up with any examples.
You Can See Everything is set to release in theatres next month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Verity is a reporter for CBC in Montreal. She previously worked for the Globe and Mail, Toronto Star and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal.

articles.title: Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
articles.summary: Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether simply creating more provinces is the solution.

image.caption: Supporters of creating more provinces say Pakistan's four existing provinces have become too large and centralized [FILE: April 2026]Image: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

blocks.text: A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people.

Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and development, recently called for a national political debate on administrative reform. He proposed creating 12 to 15 new provinces or setting up 160 empowered district governments to improve governance and the delivery of public services.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who first raised the idea of an administrative "reset" in July, said on Saturday that any new administrative units should be created with public support.
Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, meanwhile, has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots.
Despite the growing calls to create new provinces, no formal decision has been taken.
Even within the ruling coalition, there is disagreement over how and when such reforms should be pursued.
There are also questions about whether creating smaller provinces improves governance, or whether devolving power directly to local governments would be more effective.
Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute
More provinces, better governance?
Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether creating more provinces is the solution.

"Smaller provinces are not a substitute for empowered local governments. Even with smaller provinces, you will still need empowered local governments to make the system effective and improve service delivery to the people," Miftah Ismail, a former finance minister and economist, told DW.
Supporters of creating more provinces argue that Pakistan's four existing provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan — have become too large and overly centralized.
Iqbal, the planning minister, has argued that the existing system has not delivered adequate improvements in health, education, and other social services.
Interior Minister Naqvi, on the other hand, has called for an administrative structure that is better suited to Pakistan's growing population.
But there is disagreement over the solution.

"Without effective local governments, whether there is one province or 25, decision-making will remain centralized at the provincial level," Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank, told DW.

He said any proposal for new provinces or administrative units should be assessed against potential improvements in local tax collection and the costs of creating new provincial institutions, including secretariats, assemblies, and bureaucracies.
Suleri stressed that it should also be examined whether such changes would deliver justice and public services more effectively.
Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war?
Altering the political balance

"Pakistan's history suggests that empowering local governments is a better choice in terms of governance and provision of services," Muhammad Shoaib, a political scientist and assistant professor at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, told DW.
The debate, therefore, is not simply about how many provinces Pakistan should have, but whether creating smaller units would actually make the government more responsive to citizens.
Creating new provinces could also affect the political balance in the country.
New provinces would mean new governments and assemblies, while potentially changing political representation and the distribution of federal resources.
Any attempt to redraw boundaries could also reopen disputes over water, taxation, and natural resources.

The political resistance is already tangible. Sindh's provincial assembly has opposed creating new provinces or administrative units in the province, while political groups have warned against dividing existing territories.
Why Pakistan may be too reliant on EU trade
A risky strategy?
Shoaib said dividing resources would present a major challenge, even if all provinces were reorganized at the same time.
"Even if all provinces are divided simultaneously, the division of resources like finances, water, and jobs, and special privileges for territories within provinces will be a challenge," he said.
"Challenges like these require lengthy negotiations and compromises for political consensus," he added.
The issue is therefore not only about administrative efficiency, as redrawing provincial boundaries could also redistribute political and economic power.
Ismail believes redrawing provincial boundaries would be risky, particularly in Sindh.
He said empowering existing local governments within current provincial boundaries would be a safer option.

"We can learn from the US and the southern states of India, where empowered small administrative units, while competing with each other, are more responsive to citizens and deliver better services," Ismail said.

Shoaib said Pakistan could also learn from other countries, particularly democratic systems that have empowered local governments and taken time to work through the division of large states into smaller units.
"In Pakistan's case, the risk of resistance and perpetual resentment is real. A partially finished division will aggravate existing ethnic tensions," he said.
For Pakistan, the debate is therefore about more than whether the country should have four provinces or 12 or 15.

It is about whether changing the administrative map can actually bring power, resources, and accountability closer to its people, and whether such a transformation can be achieved without creating new political and ethnic tensions.

articles.title: Senior citizen arrested for stabbing neighbor over alleged hex, threat
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines – Police arrested a 62-year-old senior citizen on Monday morning, September 7, after he allegedly stabbed his neighbor in Sitio Laray Panagdait, Barangay Kasambagan, Cebu…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines – Police arrested a 62-year-old senior citizen on Monday morning, September 7, after he allegedly stabbed his neighbor in Sitio Laray Panagdait, Barangay Kasambagan, Cebu City.
The attack followed a dispute over a perceived death threat and a suspected illness-inducing hex (barang).

According to the Mabolo Police Station, the attack occurred at 7:15 a.m. on September 7. The victim, 56, was riding a motorcycle with his child on their way to buy medicine when the suspect suddenly intercepted them. The initial report didn’t indicate the child’s age.
The suspect remains in custody at the Mabolo Police Station and may face a physical injury or frustrated homicide charge, depending on the victim’s medical outcome.

articles.title: US Open: Linda Noskova edges Kostyuk, advances to quarterfinals
articles.summary: Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova reached the quarterfinals of the US Open on Sunday, edging Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk in three sets. The Czech Noskova, who has largely flown under the radar in…

blocks.text: Czech Republic’s Linda Noskova reacts as she plays Uktaine’s Marta Kostyuk in their women’s singles round of 16 tennis match on day eight of the US Open tennis tournament at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in New York on September 6, 2026. (Photo by LEONARDO MUNOZ / AFP)
Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova reached the quarterfinals of the US Open on Sunday, edging Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk in three sets.

The Czech Noskova, who has largely flown under the radar in New York despite winning Wimbledon, beat Kostyuk 7-5, 5-7, 6-4, finally sealing the win on her sixth match point when Kostyuk netted a backhand return.
“I am more than relieved,” Noskova said after booking a last-eight showdown with two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka. “This match was so tough, emotionally more so than physically.”
After a hard-fought first set, Noskova, seeded sixth, appeared poised for a relatively straightforward win, holding two match points while serving for the second set up at 5-4.
But Kostyuk, who has won two titles in 2026, slapped a forehand winner on the first and saved the second by drilling a ball at Noskova, who was at the net and couldn’t handle the volley.
Riding momentum and loud crowd support in Louis Armstrong Stadium, Kostyuk went on to take the next two games to force a third set.
In the third set, the Czech scored a key break at 3-3.
But with Noskova serving at 5-4, Kostyuk saved three more match points but couldn’t return a strong serve from Noskova, who fell to her knees after finally finishing the two-hour and 27-minute match.
Noskova took a bathroom break after the second set, as she did in the Wimbledon final against fellow Czech Karolina Muchova when she also found herself in a third set after squandering match points.
“I just had to leave the court. There was a lot of noise, but obviously I had to restart. I had to refocus, kind of put it behind me, which was not easy at all,” Noskova said.
“It’s always the most important thing to kind of get yourself back mentally after such opportunities, either in Wimby or here.”
Kostyuk said after the match that she has been playing with a right wrist injury and planned to get an MRI now that the tournament is over.
“I wasn’t 100 percent for sure,” said Kostyuk, who smiled in the later stages of the second as the crowd “started going crazy” as she saved match points.

“I’ve never had the whole stadium cheer for me like this, and it was so loud, and yeah, I wanted to soak it in, and it kept going until the rest of the match,” she said. “So it was incredible. So nothing else but smile about it.”
Kostyuk, a vocal critic of the Russian invasion of Ukraine who has spoken of the toll on her family, said she enjoyed the atmosphere despite losing.

“I just lost a match. Of course, it’s a Grand Slam. It was very close match, but I’m very happy, and nothing about the result of the match is gonna change it,” Kostyuk said. “It’s just a tennis match. I mean, come on, all good.”

articles.title: EU's Von der Leyen pledges $232 million Greenland investment
articles.summary: The EU is preparing a major investment package and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory amid Donald Trump's demand for greater US control of the mineral-rich island.

image.caption: Von der Leyen (right) said the visit was about further cementing a unique partnership with the regionImage: Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has pledged €200 million ($232 million) investment package for Greenland as the EU seeks closer relations with the Arctic territory.

Von der Leyen has been visiting Nuuk, the capital of thje Danish autonomous island, for the past two days where she met with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic counterpart Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Von der Leyen's visit comes after threats of US annexation earlier this year by President Donald Trump.
What von der Leyen said?
"Territorial integrity sovereignty, the inviolability of borders, these are fundamental principles of international law," von der Leyen told a joint press conference.
The EU chief announced the "EU-Greenland Partnership Package," focusing on three priorities: connectivity, clean energy and critical raw materials.
"This is 200 million euros of new investments for Greenland for this year and the next," von der Leyen said.
She emphasized that "Greenland's future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide, no one else."
The European Commission head arrived in Nuuk on Sunday in a show of support for Greenland and Denmark, and was received by Nielsen and Frederiksen.

"We’re deepening our cooperation across the board. Connectivity, clean energy, critical raw materials. And of course, more opportunities for the people of Greenland," Von der Leyen said in a post on X.
What does the EU investment package include?
The EU package is expected to include hundreds of millions of euros in investment in:

items: critical minerals
satellite communications
renewable energy

blocks.text: Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the visit as an opportunity to deepen the territory's "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.
The largely autonomous Greenland left the EU in 1985, although its population of about 57,000 are EU citizens through Danish citizenship.
Why is Trump demanding 'total access' over Greenland?

Von der Leyen's visit comes as the Arctic gains strategic importance for the US, Russia, China and Europe, with melting sea ice opening new shipping routes and increasing access to the region's mineral resources.

Trump has repeatedly stated that the US "needs" Greenland for its "national security," pointing to his claims — without providing evidence — that the island is "covered with Chinese and Russian ships all over the place."
Trump has maintained that Denmark cannot adequately defend the island against China and Russia.

His campaign bid to gain "total access" to the Danish territory has strained US-European relations and raised tensions within NATO as both Greenland and the Danish government have rejected Trump's demands.

articles.title: PH eyes duty-free banana exports to Japan
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Manila is seeking zero tariffs on Philippine bananas entering Japan, where the country already supplies about 80 percent of imports but still faces duties of as much as 18…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Manila is seeking zero tariffs on Philippine bananas entering Japan, where the country already supplies about 80 percent of imports but still faces duties of as much as 18 percent.

If secured, the concession would mark a significant improvement from the current terms under the Japan-Philippines Economic Partnership Agreement (Jpepa), under which Philippine bananas face an 8-percent tariff during Japan’s summer season and 18 percent during winter.

“In the end, (we want) zero tariffs,” Trade Secretary Cristina Roque told reporters on the sidelines of the Asean Business Media Exchange on Monday. “That’s what we want, but let’s wait for the final (agreement). What’s important is they’re already open to the talks.”

Securing lower tariffs is crucial for Manila because the Philippines holds a dominant share of the Japanese banana market, supplying about 80 percent of Japan’s annual imports, which total roughly 1 million tons.
Other exporters, including Thailand and Vietnam, already enjoy zero or preferential tariffs on their banana shipments to Japan.
Roque said she expects duty-free access to further strengthen the Philippines’ position in the global banana market, potentially becoming the world’s top exporter of the fruit.
Tariffs on cars
In 2025, the Philippines ranked as the world’s second-largest banana exporter behind Ecuador, with shipments surging by about 26 percent to 2.93 million metric tons (MT) from 2.33 million MT in 2024.
Asked what the Philippines would offer Japan in exchange for more favorable treatment of bananas, Roque pointed to motor vehicles.

Under the current Jpepa, only vehicles with engine displacements exceeding 3.0 liters qualify for duty-free or preferential tariff treatment, while internal combustion engine vehicles with smaller engines remain subject to a 20-percent tariff.
Roque stated that “if everything goes as planned,” they could sign the revised JPEPA in November.

Roque stated that “if everything goes as planned,” they could sign the revised JPEPA in November. Negotiations on the review began in early August, led by Trade Undersecretary Allan Gepty, the Philippines’ chief trade negotiator.
“So far, everything is going smoothly and as planned,” Roque said.
Signed in 2006 and implemented in 2008, Jpepa was the Philippines’ first bilateral FTA. It covers trade in goods and services, investments, movement of people and economic cooperation. /pai

articles.title: Manila Water eyes completing San Juan Reservoir by end of 2026
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — As climate-related challenges and natural hazards become more frequent and severe, Manila Water is strengthening the resilience of its water supply infrastructure through the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — As climate-related challenges and natural hazards become more frequent and severe, Manila Water is strengthening the resilience of its water supply infrastructure through the ongoing construction of the new San Juan Reservoir, a critical facility designed to withstand major earthquakes and support reliable water service for decades to come.

Targeted for completion by the end of 2026, the new 56-million-liter (ML) reservoir will replace the existing San Juan Reservoir and serve as a more robust and resilient water storage facility for communities in Metro Manila. Designed in accordance with modern engineering standards, the new reservoir incorporates upgraded structural, electrical, instrumentation, and mechanical systems that will help ensure uninterrupted service even in the face of increasing environmental and seismic risks.

The project forms part of Manila Water’s continuing investments to modernize and future-proof its water infrastructure amid growing challenges posed by urbanization, extreme weather events, and natural disasters.
The replacement project was pursued following extensive structural assessments of the existing San Juan Reservoir, which was originally constructed in 1968.

Engineering studies conducted by DCCD Engineering Corporation in 2011 and 2016 identified significant deterioration in the facility’s roof slab and walls resulting from decades of service. The assessments also indicated a high risk of structural failure during major seismic events, including a potential 7.2-magnitude earthquake.

In addition, the reservoir’s top slab had undergone several repairs due to holes and other defects that could potentially compromise the quality and safety of stored water supplying the San Juan Pumping Station.
Recognizing the need to enhance the long-term reliability and disaster resilience of the facility, Manila Water moved forward with the replacement of the aging reservoir.

With a total project cost of more than ₱970 million, the undertaking covers the demolition of the existing reservoir and the design and construction of the new 56-ML facility, including all associated electrical, instrumentation, mechanical, and site development works.
As of July 2026, construction progress has reached 84 percent, with work continuing toward the project’s targeted completion by the end of the year.

Once operational, the new San Juan Reservoir will strengthen the reliability of water supply service while providing greater resilience against earthquakes and other hazards that could affect critical water infrastructure.

“By investing in more resilient facilities, such as the San Juan Reservoir, we are enhancing our ability to continue delivering safe, reliable, and uninterrupted water service to the communities we serve, even during disruptive events,” Manila Water Corporate Communications Group Head Dittie Galang said.

The new San Juan Reservoir underscores Manila Water’s commitment to building infrastructure that not only meets growing water demand but also strengthens the resilience of the East Zone’s water supply system in an increasingly hazard-prone environment.

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — Electric cooperatives in Eastern Visayas warned consumers Monday, Sept. 7, of possible power interruptions as the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) placed the Visayas grid under red and yellow alerts due to tight power supply.
NGCP said it may implement Manual Load Dropping (MLD) from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. in areas served by the following distribution utilities and electric cooperatives:

items: Leyte Electric Cooperative II (Leyeco II)
Southern Leyte Electric Cooperative (Soleco)
Don Orestes Romualdez Electric Cooperative Inc. (Dorelco)
Leyeco III
Leyeco IV
Leyeco V
Eastern Samar Electric Cooperative (Esamelco)
Biliran Electric Cooperative (Bileco)
Northern Samar Electric Cooperative (Norsamelco)
Samar I Electric Cooperative (Samelco I)
Samar II Electric Cooperative (Samelco II)

blocks.text: About one million member-consumers are served by these distribution utilities across the region.
The possible power interruptions are intended to help protect the stability of the power grid amid limited generation and power imports from Mindanao, NGCP said.
The Visayas grid was placed under red alert from 6 p.m. to 7 p.m. and yellow alert from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. to 9 p.m.
NGCP reported available capacity of 2,530 megawatts (MW) against a projected peak demand of 2,508 MW, leaving only a slim reserve.

It attributed the tight supply situation to the unavailability of the large coal-fired plants TVI 1 and PEDC 3, the 146.2-MW derating of THVI 2 due to a main steam problem, and limited power imports from Mindanao.
Eight power plants were on forced outage, while 15 others were operating at reduced capacity, resulting in a total of 818.9 MW of unavailable capacity.
NGCP said the MLD schedule may still be canceled if system conditions improve, such as when actual electricity demand falls below projections.

A red alert means available supply is insufficient to meet demand and the grid’s regulating requirement, while a yellow alert indicates that the operating margin is insufficient to meet the grid’s contingency requirement.
NGCP urged consumers to use electricity prudently, particularly during peak hours. /mcm

articles.title: Marcos’ critics should be silent after Romualdez’ arrest, says Lacson
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The arrest of former House Speaker and presidential cousin Rep. Martin Romualdez should hush President Marcos’ critics, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said on Monday evening. “With the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The arrest of former House Speaker and presidential cousin Rep. Martin Romualdez should hush President Marcos’ critics, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said on Monday evening.

“With the arrest of his cousin, former Speaker Romualdez, the President’s critics who have accused him of weak leadership and a lack of resolve in confronting the flood-control mess should now be silenced by his actions,” Lacson stated in a social media post.
“Let the trial proceed and let the evidence speak. Most importantly, the former Speaker is now given his day in court,” Lacson also said.

In his last State of the Nation Address, Marcos vowed that the cases against his cousin in connection with the flood control mess would still be pursued. This is amid accusations that Marcos is shielding his allies in the corruption scandal, and instead targeting the opposition.

At 7:20 p.m., Romualdez was arrested at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for plunder after supposedly receiving P7.44 billion worth of kickbacks from government projects, including flood control infrastructure from 2022 to 2025.
At around 4 p.m., hours before the news of his arrest, Romualdez was rushed to the hospital after a “cardiovascular event” and a panic attack, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.

Lacson also commended the Office of the Ombudsman, which filed the plunder case against the congressman earlier today, saying, “The Ombudsman likewise deserves all the praise and support from the Filipino people.”
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla previously characterized Romualdez as a “central figure” in the flood control mess, noting that it would be difficult to go against plentiful resources.
It was government contractors Curlee and Sarah Discaya in 2025 who first linked the former Speaker to the infrastructure anomalies.
According to the Discayas, Quezon Rep. Marvin Rillo introduced Romualdez to them as his close friend when Rillo demanded kickbacks in exchange for government contracts.

In early 2026, two witnesses linked the Discaya couple to Romualdez, alleging that a broker for a South Forbes Park home had introduced them to Curlee Discaya, who said it was the former House Speaker who bought the property.

Romualdez previously denied having any role in the flood control scheme, with his lawyers pressing that the congressman had been prejudged by the Ombudsman as a mastermind figure in the infrastructure ordeal. /cb

articles.title: Senate approves merit scholarship program for top graduates
articles.summary: MANILA – The Senate on Monday approved a bill seeking to establish a permanent national scholarship program for outstanding senior high school graduates pursuing college or technical-vocational…

blocks.text: MANILA – The Senate on Monday approved a bill seeking to establish a permanent national scholarship program for outstanding senior high school graduates pursuing college or technical-vocational education.

Senate Bill No. 2410, or the proposed Presidential Merit Scholarship Program (PMSP) Act, is among the priority measures identified under the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council’s (LEDAC) Common Legislative Agenda for passage by Congress before the end of June 2027.

The measure would institutionalize the Bagong Pilipinas Merit Scholarship Program into PMSP as the government’s premier national merit-based scholarship and provide separate pathways for higher education and technical-vocational diploma programs.
Senator Joel Villanueva, principal sponsor and author of the measure, said financial circumstances should not determine whether academically gifted students can pursue their education.

“Ang talino at kakayahan ay hindi dapat maging pribilehiyo lamang ng may kaya. Ito ay yaman ng ating bayan na nararapat linangin at suportahan (Talent and ability should not be a privilege only of those who can afford it; these are national assets that must be nurtured and supported),” Villanueva said.
He said the program is designed to balance academic merit with equity by giving financially challenged but high-performing students a fair chance to secure government support.
“Merit opens the door, equity ensures that deserving students with less in life are given a fair chance to walk through it,” Villanueva said.

Under the measure, qualified senior high school graduates may pursue either undergraduate degree programs recognized by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) or technical-vocational diploma programs recognized by the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA).
Applicants must generally belong to families with a combined annual gross income not exceeding PHP2 million, subject to periodic adjustment to take into account inflation and education costs.
When qualified applicants exceed available scholarship slots, preference will be given to those from lower-income households.
For the higher education track, applicants must have attained at least a 95-percent general weighted average in Grade 11 and qualify for a priority degree program.
Technical-vocational applicants must have at least an 85-percent general weighted average and gain admission to a TESDA-recognized diploma program in a priority sector.

Priority fields include science, technology, engineering and mathematics; agriculture and fisheries; health and allied health sciences; information technology, artificial intelligence and data science; specialized teacher education; and research and innovation.
Timely release of benefits
The measure also requires CHED and TESDA, in coordination with the Department of Budget and Management, to establish clear timelines for processing and releasing scholarship benefits.
Villanueva said implementing agencies and participating schools must strictly observe the timelines and clearly communicate them to scholars.

“Hindi pakiusap ang napapanahong paglabas ng scholarship benefits. Obligasyon ito ng pamahalaan (The timely release of scholarship benefits is not a request. It is an obligation of the government),” he said.
“A scholarship that arrives too late may already mean a semester missed, an education interrupted, or an opportunity lost,” he added.
The scholarship may cover tuition and other school fees, living and relocation expenses, room and board, transportation, books, connectivity, laboratory costs and other education-related needs.

Scholars will also be required to render service in the Philippines equivalent to the number of years they benefited from the program through employment, professional practice, research, teaching, community engagement or public service.
“This is an education, jobs, and nation-building measure,” Villanueva said, adding that the public’s investment in scholars should eventually return to the country through their skills and service.
Existing scholars under the Bagong Pilipinas Merit Scholarship Program would continue receiving their benefits and would not be displaced or disadvantaged by the transition to the PMSP. (PNA)

articles.title: Matibag: Cayetano may face raps over 2019 SEA Games irregularities
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Alan Peter Cayetano may be included as a respondent in the charges that the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will recommend to the Department of Justice (DOJ) over…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Alan Peter Cayetano may be included as a respondent in the charges that the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will recommend to the Department of Justice (DOJ) over alleged irregularities in the Philippine Southeast Asian Games Organizing Committee (Phisgoc)’s hosting of the 2019 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games, according to NBI Director Melvin Matibag.
Matibag said this in an interview on Monday after announcing that the bureau is set to recommend filing cases against five members of the Phisgoc board of trustees, among others, in the coming days.

“He [Cayetano] introduced himself as the chairman. So it’s an ultra vires act. Pinakilala niyang chairman siya na parang nagpapatakbo. So posible na kasama siya,” Matibag said when asked if the senator would also be included in the case recommendation.
(He [Cayetano] introduced himself as the chairman. So it’s an ultra vires act. He introduced himself as the chairman as if he were running (Phisgoc). So it is possible that he will be included.)
The NBI director, meanwhile, did not specify what charges might be recommended against Cayetano and the Phisgoc officials.
According to Matibag, he met with two witnesses this Monday, noting that their testimonies regarding the supposed irregularities involving Phisgoc during the 2019 SEA Games strengthened the case.
He also said the bureau discovered that the P55-million SEA Games cauldron was contracted to different contractors.
“Siguradong may makakasuhan at siguradong may pagkakamali. Nakita na namin, very important ’yung kanina nakausap namin na witness,” said Matibag.
(Someone will definitely be charged, and definitely, there was an irregularity. We have seen it; the witness we spoke to earlier is very important.)
“Mas lalong dumami pa ’yung mga dokumento. I think we will need a few additional days this week para matapos namin,” he also said.
(The documents are piling up. I think we will need a few additional days this week to finish them.)
The Inquirer reached out to Cayetano about the matter but has yet to issue a statement as of press time.

Matibag earlier said that based on their initial findings, Phisgoc received around P6.7 billion in government funds, specifically from the Philippine Sports Commission, the Philippine Olympic Committee, and the Department of Budget and Management for the 2019 SEA Games.
He noted that if adding the other funds Phisgoc accepted from the private sector, the committee’s budget may reach over P10 billion. /cb

articles.title: Ilocos Sur town probes dredging near its waters
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The municipal government of Sta. Lucia said it would not tolerate unauthorized or environmentally harmful dredging within its jurisdiction, citing the need to protect…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The municipal government of Sta. Lucia said it would not tolerate unauthorized or environmentally harmful dredging within its jurisdiction, citing the need to protect marine ecosystems and the livelihoods of coastal communities.

The statement came after municipal officials inspected a dredging activity off Barangay Nangalisan on Monday, Sept. 7, to determine whether the operation falls within Sta. Lucia’s territorial waters and assess its possible environmental impact.
The initial on-site assessment showed that the dredging site was about 1,933 meters from the identified municipal boundary toward Sabangan, an area under neighboring Sta. Cruz town.

Mayor Joseph Simon Valdez, Vice Mayor Eduardo Toquero, members of the Sangguniang Bayan, barangay officials and representatives from the Municipal Engineering and Assessor’s offices joined the inspection, along with personnel from the police and Bureau of Fire Protection.

The local government said the measurement and site inspection form part of its continuing verification of the dredging operation’s exact location in relation to the boundaries of Sta. Lucia and Sta. Cruz.
Officials also documented conditions in the area and assessed the possible effects of the dredging on the coastal environment.
The municipal government said it would coordinate with concerned government agencies to determine whether the operation complies with environmental laws and other regulations. /mcm

articles.title: Loren Legarda praises enactment of stronger free college law
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — More students from poor families can now stay in school and finish their education, Sen. Loren Legarda said as she welcomed on Monday the enactment of Republic Act No. 12325,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — More students from poor families can now stay in school and finish their education, Sen. Loren Legarda said as she welcomed on Monday the enactment of Republic Act No. 12325, which strengthens the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education.

The new law, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Sept. 4, improves the tertiary education subsidy (TES) by directing assistance more deliberately toward the poorest students and recognizing that the cost of education goes far beyond tuition.

“It’s not enough that tuition is free if students have no money for fare to go to school and buy books, and then are short of money to buy food, or are forced to stop to help their families. Free college must mean that a student has a real chance not only to enroll, but to stay in school and graduate,” Legarda said in a mix of Filipino and English in a statement issued on Monday.
More focus on poor students

Legarda principally sponsored and authored Senate Bill No. 1894, which strengthened Republic Act No. 10931 by making student assistance more responsive to the actual financial burden of pursuing college or technical-vocational education.

Among its key reforms is focusing the subsidy more on students who need government assistance most, particularly senior high school graduates from Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) households who are admitted to qualified higher education or technical-vocational institutions.

The reform addresses a significant gap identified by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (Edcom II). Legarda now serves as an Edcom II commissioner, previously serving as its co-chairperson. She was also the chairperson of the Senate Committee on Higher, Technical, and Vocational Education

As Legarda points out, the share of TES beneficiaries from the poorest households fell from 70.73 percent in 2018 to 22.89 percent in 2022. Of 384,388 senior high school graduates from 4Ps households, only 4,746, or 1.23 percent, received TES as first-year beneficiaries in academic year 2024–2025.

“The data is clear. Many youths who should get aid first don’t benefit from it. We strengthened the system to make sure that more families in need will get the opportunity to let their children finish. We can’t describe an opportunity as universal if the poorest are the ones who get aid last,” Legarda said.
Regular subsidy reviews
The new law also provides for regular reviews of TES amounts so that it can respond to changes in the actual cost of education.

To make tertiary education more inclusive, state universities and colleges, local universities and colleges, and state-run technical-vocational institutions are also required to adopt Equity and Inclusion Plans.
This aims to remove barriers faced by persons with disabilities, students from geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, indigenous peoples, and learners from other disadvantaged backgrounds.

The law also establishes the Private Education Assistance Program, which will support qualified students who need financial assistance in private higher education institutions and technical-vocational schools.

Legarda pointed out that the law advances a principle she had been consistently pushing in education policy — that government must look beyond how many students enter school and focus on whether they are actually able to finish.

“We hope to ensure that no Filipino youth will lose the opportunity to get a quality education just because their families lack money. The lack of money should not be a reason for their education to be cut short and their dreams blocked,” she said. /atm

articles.title: Threatening letters revive fears among Kashmiri Pandits
articles.summary: Leaked addresses and phone numbers have reignited fears among Hindu government employees who returned to Muslim-majority Kashmir under a rehabilitation scheme.

image.caption: Kashmiri Hindus, known locally as Pandits, have long complained of a lack of security [FILE: June 2022]Image: Channi Anand/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A new wave of threatening letters targeting Kashmiri Pandits — members of the Hindu minority community who fled the Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley during a militant uprising in the 1990s — has deepened fears among those who have returned to the region as civil servants under an Indian government federal rehabilitation scheme.
The latest letters, which surfaced in the last week of August, named several employees. The letters also included their Jammu residential addresses, vehicle registration numbers and phone numbers.
Personal details exposed

"Similar threat letters surfaced in early August, but the latest contains our Jammu residential address, vehicle and phone numbers, which have also been shared on social media," Anil Koul, a government employee, told DW, urging authorities to investigate the source of the leak.

The letters have been attributed to a little-known group calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials suspect could be a front for the Pakistan-based Islamist militant outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba.

The group reportedly first surfaced in July, when it released a poster marking the death anniversary of a former militant commander. Authorities have yet to confirm the letters' authenticity or the existence of the group behind them.

The latest letters also distinguish between Pandits who never left the Valley — and are therefore "safe" — and those recruited under New Delhi's rehabilitation program, who are accused of working for "masters" outside Kashmir.
The fresh threats have also triggered a political row.

Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) president and former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, called them a "conspiracy" aimed at delaying the restoration of statehood, which the region lost in 2019.
Abdullah also questioned why Hindu officers from outside the region were not facing similar threats.
His remarks drew sharp criticism from Kashmiri Pandit groups and the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused him of being insensitive to the community's fears.
Familiar fears
Government records show 44,167 Kashmiri migrant families registered as having left since 1990 citing security concerns, of which 39,782 were Hindu.
For Pandit community representatives, however, the latest threats are part of a much longer security problem.

Sanjay Tickoo, president of the Kashmiri Pandit Struggle Committee (KPSS), said the threats should be viewed against the backdrop of targeted killings and repeated security concerns faced by Pandit government employees in the Valley. He blames security lapses and says repeated meetings with officials since a wave of killings in 2022 have failed to resolve their concerns.
"Since 2022, meetings have resulted in nothing," Tickoo told DW. He also wondered how those making the threats have access to employees' personal details.
"How are these details being posted on social media?" Tickoo asked.
Targeted killings have occurred sporadically in the years since. At least seven Kashmiri Pandits were killed by militants during a spike in violence between 2020 and 2022.
One of the starkest cases was that of Rahul Bhat, a Pandit revenue official who was shot dead inside his government office in Budgam in May 2022.
The last confirmed targeted killing of a Kashmiri Pandit was in October 2022, when Puran Krishan Bhat, an orchard farmer, was shot dead in Shopian district.
Former Jammu and Kashmir police chief S P Vaid described the latest threats as part of a familiar militant playbook.
"There is nothing new in this," Vaid told DW, calling it "a ploy by Pakistan to Islamize society." He said similar tactics had been used against migrant workers in the Valley.

The difference, this time, is the precision of the threats. Personal data that should not have been so easily accessible has been made public, and no clear explanation of how it was leaked has been provided.
Kashmir: Fears dampen celebrations at Hindu festival
The return dilemma

The KPSS estimates roughly 6,500 Pandits who never left the Valley, along with another 4,000 who have returned as government employees under a federal rehabilitation scheme, live in India-administered Kashmir.
But the reintegration of those who fled decades ago has proved challenging.
Rahul Pandita, a journalist and author of "Our Moon Has Blood Clots: A Memoir of a Lost Home in Kashmir," said the government's record on rehabilitation was inadequate.

"The BJP has had no rehabilitation policy for Kashmiri Hindus," Pandita told DW, arguing that the government employees in the Valley had returned under a policy introduced during the previous government of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh.
Some land has been returned and cases of killings investigated, he said, but "it is too little and too late."
Pandita said the bigger problem was that no government could guarantee a completely secure environment for a mass return.

"No matter what the government does, the situation will never be conducive enough for the Pandits to return," he said, arguing that as long as Islamist militancy exists in the region, Kashmiri Hindus would still be targeted.
"It's for them then to decide if they are willing to take such a risk," he said.
Beyond government employees, some Pandits who have returned and established businesses in the Valley are already living there quietly, Pandita said.
"That is the best-case scenario for Kashmiri Pandits in Kashmir Valley," he said.

blocks.caption: Pandits accuse the government in New Delhi of not doing enough to protect them from alleged Islamist threatsImage: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Security beyond protection
Sushobha Barve, executive secretary of the Center for Dialogue and Reconciliation, said the latest threats expose a wider security paradox.
"Despite claims of normalcy, a tiny group of active militants has successfully disrupted the lives of migrant families. Breaking the cycle of panic is essential," Barve told DW.
She said there was also growing political frustration over the delay in restoring Jammu and Kashmir's statehood, arguing that this grievance cut across the region.

Amitabh Mattoo, an academic and professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University who has written extensively on Kashmir, said any return of Kashmiri Pandits had to be both secure and dignified.

"The state has an essential role in ensuring their physical security and in protecting their property, cultural and other legitimate rights. But security measures alone will not suffice," Mattoo told DW.
"A sustainable return will also require patient reconciliation, engagement with local civil society, and the gradual rebuilding of inter-community trust and social and economic ties."

articles.title: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’
articles.summary:
Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’

A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and…

blocks.text: A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US.

Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups.

These legal outfits and like-minded allies have won key lawsuits on election issues, plus litigation thwarting Trump’s moves to end birthright citizenship and a $1.8bn slush fund that could have paid money to allies including January 6 rioters he deemed were unjustly charged.

Since Trump returned to power, for instance, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center have jointly filed lawsuits against Trump’s 2025 and 2026 executive orders on voting, challenging their constitutionality to set new voting rules that by law are run by the states.

Key legal briefs they filed together include an August one on behalf of several voting rights groups and local officials in two states to block Trump’s March 2026 executive order that would restrict voting by mail and authorize the US Postal Service to implement rules to that end.

Other groups that have accelerated their legal challenges to Trump’s moves to thwart voting rights and expand his executive powers in other ways, include the Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy Forward, the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the Washington Litigation Group.

Last month, for instance, 24 Democratic attorney generals and other plaintiffs filed suit to block USPS from moving forward with rules to curb mail voting and in late August won a temporary 14-day restraining order from federal judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts.

In response, the DoJ’s solicitor general John Sauer on Thursday appealed to the supreme court to lift the injunction, arguing in heated words that the freeze would create “serious, irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public”.

On 4 September Talwani made her injunction permanent, writing that implementing Trump’s order so close to the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.” She also stressed that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.”

Sauer on 6 September responded with another emergency appeal to the high court urging it permit the new USPS rules to go into effect, claiming that it “does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail.”

In a related twist, a detailed whistleblower complaint that Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut released last week alleged that the USPS has been proceeding with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement Trump’s order that could lead to “catastrophic failure” with this year’s mail-in voting.
About 50 million Americans, the majority of whom are Democrats, vote by mail, according to reports.

With the elections about two months away, the legal groups are stepping up efforts to thwart “self-serving attempts to take over the midterms”, said a former DoJ lawyer, which experts fear may create chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters.

Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, told the Guardian: “The CLC and the DDF have worked closely together on two ongoing lawsuits challenging the president’s unlawful voting executive orders that attempt to dictate election rules. We’ve teamed up in the supreme court on a brief filed by former state and federal judges, including noted conservative judges, that emphasized just how unlawful and dangerous the president’s efforts to dictate election rules are.”

Baldwin, who spent 14 years in the justice department’s civil rights division, said the CLC and the DDF have also “worked together in federal cases filed in Oregon and California to make sure that the DoJ isn’t able to seize voters’ sensitive data by making false claims about non-citizen voting. In cases around the country, the Campaign Legal Center is pushing back on the DoJ’s lawless efforts to vacuum up and aggregate sensitive data to create a national voter file of some sort.”

Further, former ambassador Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, which he co-founded in 2023, told the Guardian that since its inception the DDF has been involved in more than 300 legal cases and matters in three primary areas: elections, the rule of law and anti-corruption.

Eisen said the group, whose board boasts former federal judge and conservative stalwart J Michael Luttig and liberal-leaning ex-federal judge Nancy Gertner, likes to work in conjunction on cases with other ideologically diverse and nonpartisan groups like the CLC and the WLG because “they both have strong bipartisan credibility. It’s a big-tent approach we’ve taken with our election work.”

Eisen said Luttig and Gertner were instrumental in helping recruit dozens of former judges with bipartisan credentials to file amicus briefs on multiple matters including an August one to the supreme court opposing Trump’s 2026 executive order to curb mail voting.

For its part, the WLG this summer hired about half a dozen new lawyers to handle election-related litigation. “As the midterms approach with growing concerns about potential federal interference in elections, we’ve brought on more attorneys to be even more prepared to litigate sensitive matters under acute time pressure,” said James Pearce, a principal with the WLG.

blocks.caption: A Kentucky voter in Louisville casts her ballot. Photograph: Bryan Woolston/Reuters

blocks.text: Elsewhere, Sophia Lin Lakin, who leads the ACLU Voting Rights Project, said the group had been “pushing back” on administration efforts to seize personal voting data from states, and said the ACLU has been involved in 26 of 30 legal challenges to the administration on the issue. To date, the administration has lost 23 cases where rulings have been made.

Critics say Trump, the DoJ, the USPS and the Department of Homeland Security seem to be laying the groundwork for further attacks on the nation’s election rules, citing Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his radical plans to change voting rules.

In July in a televised speech, Trump falsely portrayed the nation’s voting system as riddled with fraud and condemned voting by mail and non-citizen voting. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” Trump claimed without evidence, even though he voted twice by mail this year.

Trump, who continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, also charged that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically minuscule, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on noncitizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that only cites 100 cases over a quarter-century.

But according to documents reviewed by the New York Times, hundreds of DHS agents have been engaged in a hunt to find noncitizens among registered voters. The chief of the DHS has said ICE agents could be sent to polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant”.
The DoJ has helped to amplify Trump’s bogus election claims with legal threats and actions.

In July, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the department’s civil rights division, wrote to officials in 50 states warning that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s [voter list] or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability”.
In August, the DoJ announced plans to send a larger-than-usual contingent of 1,000 lawyers to monitor voting nationwide, raising concerns that such large efforts could lead to voter intimidation.

And in a harbinger of coming legal fights, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform last month that the DoJ’s Ed Martin, a key election denialist in charge of pardons, was leaving to handle election-related litigation.
Former DoJ lawyers say administration threats to voting rights make opposition from legal advocates crucial.

Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the department at the start of 2025 after 18 years to found Justice Connection, a group of more than 3,000 ex-DoJ lawyers and other alumni, denounced Trump’s moves “to interfere” with elections.

“The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections, but that hasn’t stopped this president, or those he put in power at the justice department, from trying to interfere,” Young said in a statement. “We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.”

Justice Connection is working with experts in its alumni network to engage with the media, Congress and the public to highlight the justice department’s traditional role in election security and ensuring compliance with federal voting laws.
Other DoJ alumni agree that opposition to Trump’s election agenda is critical.

“These organizations are doing critical work in protecting the ability of people to vote and make their voices heard – a cornerstone of democracy,” said Michael Bromwich, a former DoJ inspector general. “The full-out assault on democracy must be addressed through the courts because Congress has proven itself unwilling and unable to check the undemocratic steps taken by the administration.”

Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney for eastern Michigan who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, said: “Large law firms sent armies of young attorneys to our nation’s airports to represent individuals caught up in Trump’s travel ban. That is not happening any more because of the ‘deals’ they negotiated with the Trump administration in his second term to support his pet causes.

“Thank goodness for groups like the Democracy Defenders Fund, which are attracting top legal talent and challenging some of Trump’s lawless activities. Their work is protecting the rights of all Americans.”

Further, Nick Brown, Washington state’s attorney general, who chairs an election protection group for the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said it has teamed up with some legal advocacy groups such as the Brennan Center, States United and the DDF to hold “strategy sessions” to prepare for potential disruptive moves by the Trump administration in the November elections.

Brown also attacked the administration’s appeal to the supreme court to move forward with Trump’s executive order on voting by mail, despite Judge Talwani’s strong concerns and Daga’s litigation against it.

He said: “As the court said, states’ compliance with this illegal order would be ‘practically impossible’ before the November elections given the unprecedented demands it would put on state and local elections officials. The chaos that would cause is exactly what Trump wants. That’s why we continue to fight for a fair and properly administered election.”
Baldwin too raised strong concerns about the DoJ’s push to get the supreme court to issue a ruling that would expedite Trump’s executive order on voting by mail.

She said: “The DoJ’s slapdash effort at getting the supreme court’s blessing to turn the USPS into a gatekeeper for mail would be a farce, if it didn’t put our fundamental right to vote in the crosshairs. Given the importance of what is at stake, the DoJ’s continued efforts are nothing more than an attempt to foist chaos on the electoral process. But they will fail.”
Other lawyers engaged in key election legal battles and other litigation voice optimism they will prevail.

Tianna Mays, the legal director of the DDF, said: “The Trump administration has declared war on the rule of law, yet our democratic guardrails are still holding. We refuse to stand by idly while this administration flouts the constitution and attempts to eviscerate our institutions.”

articles.title: 26 Filipino seafarers awaiting repatriation after Ukraine attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said in a statement Monday.
The DMW said that as of Sept. 4, the 26 Filipino seafarers safely disembarked from the vessel. The seafarers are currently awaiting transit to Moldova before their repatriation to the Philippines.

The DMW said it is coordinating with the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Philippine Embassy in Warsaw, Philippine Consulate General in Kyiv and Migrant Workers Office (MWO) in Prague to monitor the seafarers’ condition and facilitate their “safe and immediate” return, including the processing of their travel documents with Moldovan authorities and the ship owner.
Labor Attaché Llewelyn Perez said the Philippine diplomatic posts were working with Moldovan authorities and the shipowner to complete the documents needed for the crew’s return.

“The Philippine Embassy and the Philippine Consulate in Kyiv are coordinating with the relevant authorities, in partnership with the shipowner, to facilitate the processing of their travel documents,” Perez said.
The DMW said it is also coordinating with the licensed manning agency and the ship owner to address the seafarers’ immediate needs following their disembarkation.

“The DMW assures the families of the affected seafarers that it, together with its MWOs, Philippine embassies, and consulates, is facilitating the necessary arrangements for their safe return to the Philippines.” /gsg
