blocks.text: JAKARTA, Indonesia — A volcano erupted in Indonesia early Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic airports as ash drifted across western parts of the country.

The volcanic island of Anak Krakatau, located in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands, had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds at 3:53 a.m. Sunday and for 16 seconds about three hours later, Indonesia’s Geological Agency said. Closed-circuit camera footage showed lava flares from the volcano.

No casualties were reported and no evacuation order was issued. The nearest settlement is more than 16 kilometers (10 miles) away, but authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the active crater.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra’s southern tip, Indonesia’s Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.

AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as six other airports, including Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash.
Flights canceled as 170,000 passengers affected

By Sunday evening, the closure of eight airports had affected 170,000 passengers from 1,558 canceled flights, including 963 flights in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta airport alone. All eight airports were ordered closed until 8:59 a.m. Monday.
“It’s of course an inconvenience,” said Diego Urdiales, a Spanish tourist who was supposed to fly home to Madrid. “I was supposed to get input from the airline … but so far no news.”
“It’s a natural disaster, it’s a force majeure, so, what can we do?” said Michele Gouw, an Indonesian passenger. “We just have to accept it and wait for the airline and airport directions.”

Indonesia’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation said that it was closely monitoring the eruption’s impact on air travel and coordinating with airlines, airport operators, air navigation services and the meteorology agency.
“Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision,” Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement.
He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations.
The eruption also disrupted services at Bali’s I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport and at Medan.
Volcano remains active
Indonesia’s volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre identified two ash clouds using satellite imagery.

One plume rose to 20,000 feet (6,100 meters) and drifted northeast over Jakarta, Banten, West Java and nearby waters. A second cloud reached 50,000 feet (15,200 meters) and spread over parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces, the southern Sunda Strait and sections of the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra.
Lana Saria, head of Indonesia’s Geological Agency, said activity at Anak Krakatau has intensified since July, with Sunday’s eruption the strongest during that period.
The repeated eruptions indicate a continued supply of magma and volcanic gases beneath the volcano, she said, though officials can’t predict whether a larger eruption will occur.
“We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” Saria said in a video briefing.
She said the main hazards include volcanic ash, high concentrations of gas and the ejection of hot rocks and other material around the crater area.
Schools move to online learning

The eruption’s impact extended beyond air travel. The government on Sunday authorized schools in areas affected by volcanic ash could temporarily move to online learning at home. The measure is intended to reduce students’ exposure to ashfall and allow local authorities to adjust classroom activities based on conditions on the ground.
Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau,” is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.

An eruption of Anak Krakatau in 2018 caused a tsunami that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau’s southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water. Scientists said that Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption. /dl

articles.title: U.S. investigators to focus on crucial moment of touchdown in Amazon cargo plane crash

image.caption: An Amazon cargo plane sits at the Miami International Airport on Monday, after it overshot the runway on Sunday, killing five people. (Lynne Sladky/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. federal investigators examining why an Amazon cargo jet barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport and into vehicles, killing at least five people, are likely to focus on a crucial moment in the landing: whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.
It wasn't clear if the pilots were among the 5 people killed in Sunday's incident

Video of Sunday's landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Aviation experts said investigators will seek to determine exactly where the plane landed and, if it was beyond the normal touchdown zone, why the pilots did not abandon the landing and circle back for another attempt.

Investigators will also examine the plane's speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft's mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has sent a team led by chair Jennifer Homendy to Miami, where she is expected to give the agency's first briefing on the investigation Monday.

The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. ET on Sunday after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people died, three were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.
Pilots, people in cars trapped

The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and co-pilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle. It wasn't immediately clear if the pilots were among those killed.

The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 914 metres of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.

It wasn't raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
"A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you've already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away," Schiavo said.
5 dead after Amazon cargo plane leaves runway, smashes into cars
No safety system on Miami runways

The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports countrywide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.

Miami's airport appears to be in compliance and wasn't required to have an arresting system because it has a 1,000-foot (304-metre) safety buffer at the end of its runways, said Mike O'Donnell, the FAA's former director of airport safety and accident investigations.
The requirement was prompted by American Airlines Flight 1420 overrunning a runway at Little Rock National Airport in Arkansas in 1999, killing nine.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
History of aircraft

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon.

items: At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barrels off Miami runway and smashes into cars: police

blocks.text: More than 160 flights were cancelled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320 kilometres north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
Amazon said in a statement that it would co-operate with any investigation.

"We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss."

Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville's Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.

articles.title: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner hold Ukraine talks after meeting Putin
articles.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, seeking to revive efforts to end the war. But the latest diplomatic push seems to have…

image.caption: The US envoys met Zelenskyy after talking to Putin in MoscowImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held "encouraging" talks in Kyiv on Sunday during their first official visit to Ukraine, but made no breakthrough toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Despite the renewed diplomatic push, Moscow and Kyiv remain divided over key issues, particularly territorial concessions. Kushner acknowledged the challenge, saying the US was working "behind the scenes" to create the conditions for a possible deal.
"It’s a very, very hard problem, but we’re going to try," Kushner said.
As Ukraine's airspace remains closed due to the conflict, the pair arrived in Kyiv by train from Poland, having held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier.
Putin had declared a three-day ceasefire to ensure the envoys' safety.
Ukraine peace push? Trump envoys hold talks with Kremlin
Zelenskyy: We will need a 'winter package'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held three rounds of talks with the US envoys, the final one joined by national security advisers from the United Kingdom, France and Germany.

After meeting with Witkoff and Kushner, Zelenskyy said the talks focused on military aid, including Patriot missile systems and other weapons Ukraine will need in the coming months. He said Kyiv was seeking "serious volumes" of US support, with backing from its European partners.
"If the war drags on until winter — and that is how things currently look — we will need a 'winter package'," he said.
The Ukrainian president also expressed gratitude that representatives of European nations were in Kyiv.
"Here we are all on the same side," he said.
What did Russia say about Moscow talks?
Momentum by US President Donald Trump to end the four-and-a-half-year-old conflict has stalled in recent months after talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January failed to produce a result.
Despite hopes of a breakthrough with the Russian leader on Saturday, there were no announcements after the meeting.
Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described the Moscow talks as constructive, frank, and useful but didn't discuss specific outcomes.
Ushakov said the talks also focused on economic issues and potentially large Russia-US projects.
During previous talks, negotiators have struggled to bring both sides together on a range of key issues, including the future of the industrial Donbas region of eastern Ukraine.

blocks.caption: The US and Russia have been discussing tie-ins for months to try and end the warImage: Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukraine war escalating in recent months
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and Washington are crucial to deterring Russia ​from further aggression.
Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, told the New York Times last weekend that he did not expect the fighting to end before spring 2027.
He also predicted further Russian strategic air strikes on Ukraine this winter.
The war has escalated in recent months, with Putin seeking the complete conquest of Donbas and Russian drones targeting the Ukrainian capital.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has focused its drone attacks on Russia's energy sector. It has also targeted online retailers deep inside Russia to try and bring the war home to the public.

articles.title: Can the AfD form a government in Saxony-Anhalt?
articles.summary: Following its record election success, the far-right Alternative for Germany aims to form a government. What options does it have without a majority?

image.caption: The AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has led his party to an unprecedented win in Saxony-AnhaltImage: Michael Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved its best-ever election result in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, winning well over 40% of the vote and leaving all other parties far behind.

However, the party lacks the majority of seats in parliament needed to govern on its own. Because the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as "confirmed far-right extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency, other parties announced that cooperation with the AfD was out of the question. This will make forming a government in this eastern German state quite difficult.

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund announced on public broadcaster ARD: "As a democrat, I will reach out to all those who wish to work with us to bring about a fundamental political turnaround." At the same time, he acknowledged that there are currently no political parties that he considers suitable for a coalition government.

Above all, he was referring to the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds power in coalitions both in Saxony-Anhalt and on the federal level in Germany. Siegmund, along with the entire AfD leadership, has characterized the CDU's policy of refusing to work with the AfD a failure.

On public broadcaster ZDF, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel sharply criticized the CDU for stonewalling the AfD: "The CDU will not win another election — not a federal election. And this clearly gives the AfD a mandate to govern. Because we are democrats, we do not refuse to work with others."

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund emphasized that implementing the AfD's platform was more important to him than the prospect of power: "There will be no compromise with me." Leading up to the vote, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate repeatedly stated that he was only interested in governing alone in order to usher in a fundamental political change in Germany.
The AfD's radical governing platform

For months, the AfD's political program has sparked heated debates across Germany. That's because the party wants to drastically tighten asylum and immigration policies. It wants to speed up the deportation of illegal asylum seekers and introduce a general work requirement for all other asylum seekers.

Above all, however, it wants to make Saxony-Anhalt and Germany less attractive to immigrants and is calling for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy." During its election campaign, the party repeatedly blamed migrants for crime in German cities and for the housing shortage.

What's more, the AfD is planning a radical restructuring of society: it has declared war on public broadcasting, wants to cut funding for democracy projects, intends to establish a kind of vigilante group against migrants and aims to combat social diversity — all of which is laid out in its platform. And Ulrich Siegmund emphasized in an ARD interview that these issues are non-negotiable.
Now, one option involves a minority government led by the AfD, in which it would need to secure support from other parties to advance its policies.
AfD: Saxony-Anhalt result will 'shake all of Germany'
AfD Chairwoman Alice Weidel told ZDF television: "Who ultimately forms the government — perhaps through a tolerance agreement or even a coalition — remains to be seen."
On behalf of the CDU, the party's secretary-general, Franziska Hoppermann, categorically ruled out a coalition: "There will be no cooperation with the far left or the far right."
Could the BSW help the AfD form a government?
The biggest unknown in this power struggle is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), should it manage to move into the state parliament.

The small party campaigns primarily on a left-wing economic platform and — similar to the AfD — calls for a foreign policy that is more friendly toward Russia. In the past, party founder and former member of the socialist Left Party, Sahra Wagenknecht, has repeatedly expressed openness to substantive cooperation with the AfD. However, for ideological reasons, the party is not considered a particularly attractive partner within AfD circles.

As the AfD celebrated its victory into the night and even before the vote count was complete, some AfD state politicians announced that, if necessary, they intended to remain in the opposition and keep the other parties on the defensive until they could secure a majority of their own.

Take, for example, Oliver Kirchner, co-chair of the AfD caucus in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt: "If we end up behind the lectern as the opposition, it will be brutal for the others," he warned during an AfD livestream.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: How Runa Khan’s ‘snowball’ of change started from a hospital ship
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Listening to people’s needs is where change begins, and seeking people with empathy to witness its impact is where it “snowballs.” This is according to Bangladeshi humanitarian…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Listening to people’s needs is where change begins, and seeking people with empathy to witness its impact is where it “snowballs.”
This is according to Bangladeshi humanitarian and social entrepreneur Runa Khan, who was recently honored with the Ramon Magsaysay (RM) Award, widely regarded as the “Nobel Prize of Asia.”

The Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation recognized the 67-year-old founder and executive director of nongovernmental organization Friendship for “her profound empathy for the poorest of the poor in her country, and her courage, vision, and tenacity in building and leading Friendship to accomplish her mission.”

“In her hands, privilege became not an entitlement, but a responsibility; not a family legacy to protect, but a gift to be shared so that others, too, might have the chance to live with hope, opportunity, and dignity,” it said in its citation.
Starting with one floating hospital in 2002, Khan built Friendship into a full-scale social purpose organization, providing services impacting more than 7.5 million people today.
Friendship currently has seven hospital ships, two land-based hospitals, 550 mobile clinics, and 700 trained Friendship community medic aides, serving riverine, coastal, and refugee communities.

“I started the work because I just couldn’t leave or not be responsible for what was staring at me in the face, which was incredible poverty. But 25 years ago, these ideas were totally untouched,” Khan said in a Zoom call with the media on Thursday.
Access to healthcare
The first hospital ship Friendship established came from the recognition that people who have nothing still need access to healthcare.

“Without access to health, you can’t provide a person, any kind of empowerment to a person, or any kind of hope to a person, nor give them dignity, and for me this is extremely important,” Khan told the Inquirer.

Asked how she would inspire the Philippines, she said she would seek out people with empathy and the ability to mobilize funding, and bring them to Bangladesh to witness the impact of Friendship’s work.
Khan said the solution need not necessarily be a mobile hospital ship; what matters is a holistic healthcare system that ensures no one is left behind.
She started with healthcare, then realized the need for other services such as education and climate adaptation, saying “it came from the needs of the community” and listening to what people said.
Friendship has constructed prefabricated schools that can be dismantled within hours and reassembled elsewhere when erosion poses a threat.
These schools have served nearly 30,000 students, who achieved an impressive average score of 90.05 percent in Bangladesh’s Secondary School Certificate examinations.
Through their climate adaptation operations, they have built solar villages and afforested over 200 mangrove hectares, with 10,000 volunteers in training for rescue and relief.
Beyond work
Khan’s approach to development grew from listening to people’s needs and believing that those who witnessed the impact would become advocates for it.
“I thought if I could get people, you know, if I could make that one person believe and trust, I wanted them to come to see it and then they would be the voice,” she said.
“If you ask me how it snowballed, it snowballed because of the work; my colleagues, they are incredible,” she added, crediting them for their leadership as well.
Khan said she considers the people in Friendship more like family than staff, adding that they have never viewed their work simply as a job, but beyond that.
Khan said millions of people still live with so few resources that even minute changes in the climate can overwhelm their ability to cope.
For vulnerable communities living in areas highly exposed to extreme weather, even a small change in the climate can become a “thin line between life and death for them,” she said.

Khan pointed to the importance of mangroves as a natural defense against storm surges and rising seas, particularly in coastal communities where the loss of mangrove forests has left people increasingly exposed.
Today, Khan runs Bangladesh’s largest private mangrove reforestation and nursery program, helping shield vulnerable coastal communities from extreme weather.

Friendship is also building raised plinths that serve as flood shelters for displaced families, their belongings and livestock, equipped with safe drinking water, washrooms and other basic facilities.
‘Hope for tomorrow’
Khan has spent years working among people whose lives are shaped by poverty and an increasingly unpredictable climate.
Yet when asked what young people can do in the face of problems as enormous as climate change, she does not begin with the global picture.
“You can’t deal with macro if you don’t know how to use the micro,” said Khan, encouraging the youth to pursue change they can sustainably do.
For her, wealth has little to do with how much a person can accumulate, saying “the richness of your life is how you use what you have.”
“Don’t spoil your spirit, your soul, your life of peace and comfort running after that [money]. You need it, but please harmonize that with also giving,” she said.
Khan encourages people to set aside even 2 percent of their money for charity, while stressing, “You have to be able to save some money that gives you the courage to hope for tomorrow.” /cb

articles.title: Trailblazing Indigenous actor and director Georgina Lightning dies
articles.summary: Indigenous filmmaker and actor Georgina Lightning has died at the age of 63. Her daughter, Crystle Lightning, announced the news online late Saturday night, just before 11 p.m., though no details…

image.caption: Indigenous storyteller and filmmaker Georgina Lightning has died at the age of 63. This image shows her in one of her projects, Trickster, which aired on CBC. (Georgina Lightning as Sophia in Trickster.)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

Indigenous filmmaker and actor Georgina Lightning has died at the age of 63. Her daughter, Crystle Lightning, announced the news online late Saturday night, just before 11 p.m., though no details about the cause of death were shared.
Daughter confirms Lightning's death in social media post Saturday night
Indigenous filmmaker and actor Georgina Lightning has died at the age of 63.
Her daughter, Crystle Lightning, announced the news online late Saturday night, just before 11 p.m., though no details about the cause of death were shared.

Social media posts link her death to the Enoch Indian Relay World Championship at the Enoch Park Race Track, an event Lightning posted about on her Facebook page just one day before her death was made public.

Enoch Cree Nation announced in a statement on Saturday that it “is mourning the loss of a community member following an incident that occurred during [Saturday’s] Indian relay event.” The nation did not confirm the identity of the person who died.
RCMP told CBC News Sunday that officers were called to the Enoch Park Race Track shortly after 6:30 p.m., where a woman had died before police arrived.
Police said the woman who was killed was standing in the media area, but would also not confirm her identity.
RCMP said that Occupational Health and Safety will take over the investigation.
Born in Edmonton, Lightning was a member of the Samson Cree Nation, located about 100 kilometres south of the city.
In addition to her impact in the film industry, she was widely known as an outspoken advocate for First Nations causes.
More to come.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Kelsie Johnston is a reporter for CBC Edmonton. She previously worked as an associate producer for The Decibel at The Globe and Mail. She can be reached at kelsie.johnston@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Digesting the AfD's landmark election win
articles.summary: With well over 40% for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), Saxony-Anhalt has witnessed a landmark election night. DW's reporters were on the ground.

image.caption: The AfD's Alice Weidel, Ulrich Siegmund and Tino Chrupalla were jubilant on Sunday eveningImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: After an unusually quiet evening at the press center for the Saxony-Anhalt state election, journalists, camera crews and technicians were suddenly running around, jostling and shouting. Ulrich Siegmund, the leading candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), went running off with his bodyguards, looking for the best place to stand so that he would be clearly visible on camera when the election projections started appearing on the screens.

And then, a few minutes later, the commotion started up again, as AfD party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla arrived, beaming just as broadly as Siegmund. Another scramble ensued, and the bodyguards shouted: "Stay back!"

At 6 pm, when the preliminary results finally came in, the AfD was well above 40%. For the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which governs the region between the Elbe and the Harz Mountains, it is a nightmare — there's no other way to put it. Weidel subsequently declares the result a clear mandate for her party to form a government. It's hard to disagree with her on that. She tells reporters that even before Christmas rolls around, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) will be replaced following this election result.
Weidel: 'This is a mandate for us to form a government!'
After all, Merz, whose popularity has hit record lows across the country, was rarely seen during this election campaign. And his party here in Saxony-Anhalt was glad about that.

AfD co-chair Tino Chrupalla also spoke of a blow to the chancellor, who he said only makes grandiose announcements. He also accused the chancellor of "unnecessarily escalating" tensions with Russia recently. Once the cameras were off, Chrupalla admitted that even he hadn't expected such a clear victory.

The AfD, which the domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed far-right extremist," held its election party at the Altes Theater, just a stone's throw from the press center. Before entering the building, journalists and visitors were searched by police dogs, and bags were checked twice.

"This feels less like a state election and more like a G7 summit," said DW correspondent Matthew Moore, after finally getting into the Altes Theater. To maintain order over the weekend, 1,800 additional police officers were dispatched to Saxony-Anhalt from other federal states.
'Like a trip to the dentist': The CDU at the Maritim Hotel

And what about the CDU, which has governed Saxony-Anhalt for the last 24 years? The voters' rejection of the party could hardly be more decisive. That Sven Schulze, the incumbent premier, did not resign immediately could even be seen as an act of bravery. With a stony expression, he told his supporters: "This is democracy!"

At the beginning of the year, Schulze succeeded Reiner Haseloff as head of government in Saxony-Anhalt. Seventy-two-year-old Haseloff was highly respected in the state and yet did not wish to run for another term. But when he stepped down, it was too late for Schulze to counter the force of support for the AfD.

The CDU election party — which turned out to be not much of a party at all — was held at the four-star Maritim Hotel. In the hotel ballroom, only die-hard CDU supporters remained to witness the debacle. This year's results were half of what they were in the previous state election. It was a difficult defeat for the party that remained the strongest political force in Saxony-Anhalt for the last twenty years. "It's a bit like being in the dentist's waiting room," a CDU supporter told DW reporter Bernd Riegert with a bitter smile. "You know it's going to hurt, but you can't run away."
Uncertainty regarding the BSW

No matter how big the right-wing populists' election victory may be, the AfD has little chance of governing with an absolute majority. And so far, all other parties have ruled out entering into a coalition with it.
It will likely come down to the economically left-wing and politically conservative Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which could narrowly make it into the state parliament.

Meanwhile, Eva von Angern, the leading candidate for the socialist Left Party in Saxony-Anhalt, spoke of a "dark day" for the state, because of "the consequences this result could have for Saxony-Anhalt and the people of Saxony-Anhalt." And by that, she was also referring to the AfD's hardline policy toward refugees. During the campaign, the AfD made it clear time and again that asylum seekers whose applications were rejected would be deported on a large scale "from day one."
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Hope within the SPD for a majority without the AfD

As for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the junior partner in Chancellor Merz's federal government struck a surprisingly optimistic tone. Despite predictions that they would fare much worse, the Social Democrats are now assured of representation in the state parliament. In distant Berlin, SPD Secretary-General Tim Klüssendorf was not yet ready to give up hope that a coalition of all mainstream parties might be able to bypass the AfD and form a coalition: "If such a majority exists, then it should be formed with the participation of all the parties represented in this state parliament," he said.
Greens between euphoria and shock

The environmentalist Greens spent election night somewhere between euphoria and shock. Actually, the party should be delighted with such an unexpected result. Predictions had long suggested they might fail to clear the five-percent threshold, but now they're safely in. DW reporter Giula Saudelli said that some staff members at the Green Party's election party had tears in their eyes when the projections appeared on the screens: tears of relief for their own party and tears of shock at the AfD's gains.

"There's no reason to jump for joy when it's still unclear whether far-right extremists will be able to govern this state," party co-leader Felix Banaszak told DW. He had spent a lot of time campaigning in Saxony-Anhalt. Videos on social media showed him being openly attacked and verbally abused. But he continued nonetheless. People close to him say that this may have contributed to the Greens' election success — a success that doesn't quite feel like one.
… and in Berlin, the chancellor remains silent

But this much is clear: it was an historic evening in Saxony-Anhalt: a defining moment. Much remains unclear, such as who will eventually govern the state and what consequences this will have for Chancellor Friedrich Merz. A press conference has been scheduled with him for midday on Monday.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but fundamental differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
articles.summary: Despite talks between US envoys and both Putin and Zelensky, the expectation in Kyiv is the fighting will continue, writes James Landale.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
By
Diplomatic correspondent
The talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion.

The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago.

The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday.
You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making.
Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell.
And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe.

blocks.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin greets Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia

blocks.text: But fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield.

The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded.

Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army.

After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult".
Watch: President Zelensky welcomes US envoys in Kyiv
Witkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there.
But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that.
So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead.
Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic.
Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long.

articles.title: Manitoba family searches for answers nearly 2 years after daughter died following dental procedure
articles.summary: The parents of a 23-year-old woman who died after she went to have her wisdom teeth removed at a southern Manitoba dental clinic say they've been left "shattered" and searching for answers nearly two…

image.caption: Virginia Blatz, 23, died on Nov. 27, 2024 after she went to have her wisdom teeth removed at Boundary Trails Dental Centre in Morden, Man. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

blocks.text: Manitoba

The parents of a 23-year-old woman who died after she went to have her wisdom teeth removed at a southern Manitoba dental clinic say they've been left "shattered" and searching for answers nearly two years after their daughter's death.
Virgina Blatz, 23, died on Nov. 27, 2024, after going to Morden clinic to have wisdom teeth removed
Virginia Blatz was pronounced dead in hospital on Nov. 27, 2024, after going to the Boundary Trails Dental Centre in Morden, Man., to have her wisdom teeth removed that morning.

An autopsy found Virginia's death was caused by local anesthetic systemic toxicity — when levels of the pain-blocking medication become too high in a person's blood — "resulting from an inadvertent intravascular injection of local anesthetic," according to the family's lawyer Troy Harwood-Jones.
CBC News has not independently viewed the autopsy report.
Virginia's mother Victoria Blatz said her daughter was keen to get her wisdom teeth removed because she had been suffering with a sore mouth in the days leading up to the procedure.
Victoria dropped Virginia off at the dental clinic on the morning of Nov. 27, 2024, and planned to pick her up as soon as the appointment was over.
The clinic called Victoria a short time later, saying her daughter was having a seizure.
Victoria said the clinic was frenzied when she returned. It was as if she "walked into a nightmare" when she saw her daughter there, she said.
"It's obviously the worst thing I've ever seen. It's the worst experience I've ever had. It was terrible," Victoria said.
As the two-year anniversary of Virginia's death creeps closer, her father Dulaney Blatz says the family is still searching for answers about what happened in the dentist's chair.
"Maybe we will never know the truth," he said.
The Manitoba Dental Association began investigating the incident, which happened when Virginia was under the care of Dr. Ronald Janz, shortly after it occurred.

items: Southern Manitoba woman, 23, dies following dental procedure

blocks.text: Janz is still listed as a general dentist on the Boundary Trails Dental Centre's website. According to the dental association's registry, he is currently restricted in his ability to administer local anesthetic drugs.

Dulaney said the family didn't hear from the dental association until several months after Virginia's death. And they're still unsure what's happening with the investigation after many more months have passed, he said.
Victoria said the lack of answers has been "massively frustrating" for the family.

"We were a shattered family for quite some time after Virginia's death. We just really could not function properly. And we had so many questions and we were so unsure and we were really, really struggling," she said.
"We've just come to the point where we're so tired of being patient."
Southern Manitoba woman, 23, dies following dental procedure
The family filed a separate formal complaint about Janz in June.

The dental association's lawyers said in a Sept. 1 letter sent to the Blatzs' legal counsel that information about the initial investigation wasn't being shared with Virginia's loved ones because the MDA's registrar is the official complainant under rules set out in the Dental Association Act — not the family.

That letter was in response to an Aug. 21 letter sent by the family's lawyers asking for updates on the initial investigation and the status of the Blatz family's new complaint. CBC News has viewed both letters.

In a statement to CBC News on behalf of the Manitoba Dental Association, Rodrigo Sanches Cunha, the association's president, acknowledged the family's frustration, and said that while they understand why Virginia's family wants answers, they have "a legal and regulatory responsibility to conduct a thorough and fair process."
"As you can appreciate, details of the investigation cannot be shared because this matter has not reached its final adjudicative conclusion," the statement said.
"We recognize that the length of this process, together with confidentiality requirements that limit what we can share, has compounded an already unbearable situation for Virginia's family."
"We will contact them directly this week to explain where the process stands, what happens next, and what information we can appropriately share without compromising the integrity of the proceeding."
CBC News has also reached out to the Boundary Trails Dental Centre.
Dulaney said Virginia — the youngest of their five children — was set to start a new job as a welder just a few days after her final dental appointment.

items: Winnipeg man sues dental office after teeth allegedly removed during 'unauthorized surgery'

blocks.text: Her father said she was hard-working and kind, with dreams to settle down on a little farm like the one her parents run near Lowe Farm, about 70 kilometres south of Winnipeg.
"We lost a wonderful daughter who was kind and caring to everybody," he said, adding she loved people and animals dearly.
Victoria said Virginia was a "bright light" who had a happy future ahead of her.
The family wants justice for their daughter.
"We've suffered a monstrous loss and the community has suffered a monstrous loss and our family will never be the same again. It's shattered us all completely," Victoria said.
"We want answers and accountability and assurances that this is not going to happen to other families."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Scott is a Winnipeg-based reporter with CBC Manitoba. They hold a master’s degree in computational and data journalism, and have previously worked for the Hamilton Spectator and The Canadian Press.

articles.title: The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?
articles.summary: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’…
articles.byline: Ben Doherty, Andy Ball and Nick Evershed

blocks.text: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.

New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.
In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.

“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …

“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”
The US military-industrial complex in Australia
Each square represents one facility
United States-controlled facilities with Australian access (17)
Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access (24)
Australian facilities with US military access (51)
Australian facilities with US corporate access (18)
Australian facilities with no significant US access (41)
Australian facilities with US access unresolved (17)
Guardian graphic
‘Aligning ourselves completely’
The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:

items: Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.
Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.
Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.
Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.

blocks.text: Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.
Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.

Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.

Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.

Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.
Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.

Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.

blocks.caption: Workers with a missile at the Port Wakefield facility. Photograph: Lockheed Martin

blocks.text: The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.
Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.

The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.

The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.

Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.

“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.
“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”

Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.

“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”

There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.

Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.
“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”
‘Waltzing its way into a war’
At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.
Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.
“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.

blocks.caption: US defense secretary Pete Hegseth meets Australia’s defence minister Richard Marles at the Pentagon. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA

blocks.text: Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.
Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.
“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”

Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.

The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.

But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.
The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.
Australians’ fragile faith
Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.
But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.
A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.
Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.
Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).
Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.

Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).

More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.

US facility with Australian access
US corporate access
This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.
“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”

Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.

“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.
“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”
Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.
“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”

She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.
“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”

Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.

“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.
Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.
“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.
“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”

Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”

articles.title: Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
articles.summary: False and misleading claims are raising questions about the integrity of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. DW Fact Check takes a closer look.

image.caption: A voter casts a ballot in Saxony-Anhalt's state election, amid false and misleading claims alleging election fraud and irregularitiesImage: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.

In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.
DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.
Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.
Fake video shows election workers destroying AfD ballots

Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.

A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."
The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube.
Verdict: False
There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.

They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.
The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.
Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election.

blocks.caption: Though a false claim purported that AfD ballots were destroyed, the AfD in fact won a huge share of the vote on SundayImage: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russian disinfo campaign alleges CDU fraud

Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.
"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.

DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.
The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.
Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".

One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."

Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.
"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.

DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.

blocks.caption: A misleading claim alleged that postal ballots were being counted before polls closedImage: Michael Bihlmayer/Bihlmayerfotografie/IMAGO

blocks.text: Did Halle start counting ballots too early?

Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist.

Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".
Verdict: Misleading
The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.
Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.

The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."

The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting.
How close is Germany's AfD to taking power?

articles.title: Germany set to feel the impact of Saxony-Anhalt's AfD win
articles.summary: The state election could have major consequences for Germany's government. Pollsters cite dissatisfaction with Merz as one reason for the CDU's poor showing.

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (center) made few campaign appearances in Saxony-Anhalt to support CDU Premier Sven Schulze (right)Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Only 1.6 million eligible voters were called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, September 6. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

For weeks it was clear that the vote had become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

The in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the election, doubling its percentage compared to the last election five years ago, while the ruling CDU lost half of its support. If the AfD now manages to form a government, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.
How the AfD win puts pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz
Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW before the election. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

Koschmieder also predicted that a strong showing by the AfD would intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist. The CDU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.

Most analysts believe that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party.
Could a CDU government get support from the Left Party?

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.
Saxony-Anhalt election: Can the CDU stop the AfD?
Merz's determined to press ahead with controversial pension reform plans

The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. This year, he still plans to bring his controversial reforms of the old age pension system through parliament, which have been heavily criticized by members of his own party on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt.
But that hasn't discouraged Merz. "The pension system is no longer sustainable because of demographics, and we have known this for years," he said.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
SPD hopes for success in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
What about the Social Democrats? They have remained at around 8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt. This is a great improvement on what was being predicted six months ago.

In addition, the Social Democrat premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Manuela Schwesig, has good odds of a renewed mandate in state parliament elections there on September 20. The SPD has made a strong comeback in the polls in the coastal state since last year; with around 30% of the vote, they could form a government with the Left Party, the CDU or potentially both.
Why voters are so unhappy with leadership in democracies
This article was originally written in German. It was first published on September 3, and updated and republished to include the Saxony-Anhalt election results on September 6.

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong
articles.summary: The AfD has emerged as the strongest party in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt by a wide margin. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?

image.caption: Though the AfD has been classified as a 'confirmed right-wing extremist' organization, this has done little to dent its popularityImage: Klaus-Dietmar Gabbert/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage.

Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.

Saxony-Anhalt is also home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still accounts for around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the Elbe River, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.

The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.
Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.

Nevertheless, international attention is now turning to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government after the Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, won in a landslide on September 6.
Can the AfD rule the state?

The far-right AfD has taken a massive lead at the Saxony-Anhalt election, but it was not immediately clear if it will be able to form government. The party's state leader said the result sends "a signal to Berlin." The ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since German reunification in 1990, has lost half of its support. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) which has failed to secure representation by falling underneath the threshhold of 5%.
The state office for the protection of the constitution has classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters.

CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as state premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."

The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.
Saxony-Anhalt's unusual political history

From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt was also at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party.

Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?

Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.
What's driving AfD support in Saxony-Anhalt?

Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in the state feel with developments in Germany. Many jobs disappeared in the years following reunification, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.

Saxony-Anhalt also faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.

Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the state's Statistical Office, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.
What would AfD rule mean for Saxony-Anhalt?

According to many observers, the success of the far-right DVU some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy program.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?

Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of the Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded.
"I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely," he said. In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.

Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script," he said.
The new parliament will convene on October 6, the weeks leading up to this date will see difficult negotiations to form a majority for a new government.
This article was originally written in German. It was first published on August 24, and updated following the election on September 6.

articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD celebrate projected win in state election
articles.summary: AfD leaders celebrated tonight as exit polls projected a big lead in the Saxony-Anhalt vote.

blocks.text: Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is celebrating as exit polls show they are set to win more than 44% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD's projected result is higher than earlier opinion polls suggested and the party has hailed the news as a "historic outcome".
However, party leaders will not know if they have enough seats to govern until they see which of the smaller parties get into the state parliament.
That may hinge on whether one of the smaller parties gets over the required threshold of 5%.
Berlin correspondent Jess Parker reports from the AfD party HQ as supporters celebrated the projected results.

articles.title: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran
articles.summary:
Chris Wright tells ABC there ‘may not’ be an agreement that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons

US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able…

blocks.text: US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”

He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.

He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.
“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.

In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.

This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.

Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.

“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.

“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
